the commutation relations $$ [x_a, x_b] = \theta f_{abc} x_c\,, $$ with $f_{abc}$
totally antisymmetric tensors. We note that these can be brought to a diagonal
form, and propose that it is beneficial to do so in the quantum theory. The
corresponding phase-space coordinates are found, and it is shown that the
corresponding quantum mechanics is commutative and retrievable from special
cases of classical phase-space geometry. These results imply that certain
aspects of quantum field theory can be mapped to their classical (semiclassical)
relatives.
  The algebra of observables for Dirac particles on these spaces is also
studied, and it is found that its universal representation is also commutative,
with the additional bonus that its structure is isomorphic to that of the
original commuting algebra. This then implies that certain quantum spin
operators are all identical to their classical counterparts.
  Finally, it is noted that the Fock space of Dirac particles can be obtained
from a classical (semiclassical) phase space, implying that at least in this
case, (noncommutative) quantum field theory can be mapped to classical field
theory.
  In conclusion, the noncommutativity can be completely removed from Dirac
algebra and its Fock space by a suitable change of variables to diagonal
generators. All Dirac observables become commuting, and the quantum theory
reduces to its classical (semiclassical) limit.
  The present work extends to the Dirac case previous similar findings for
Maxwell theory and its relation to classical (electromagnetism). It also
completes the program of investigating quantum theories on various
noncommutative spaces characterized by different types of spatial
commutation relations.
  It would be interesting to investigate whether the results found here for
Dirac particles can be extended to more general spin theories.
  Finally, it would be interesting to further investigate the phase space
characterization of phase spaces corresponding to any given set of commuting
generators.

  We propose a new time-varying econometric model, called Time-Varying Poisson
AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX), suited to model and forecast
time series of counts. We show that the score-driven framework is particularly
suitable to recover the evolution of time-varying parameters and provides the
required flexibility to model and forecast time series of counts characterized
by convoluted nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. We study the asymptotic
properties of the TV-PARX model and prove that, under mild conditions, maximum
likelihood estimation (MLE) yields strongly consistent and asymptotically normal
parameter estimates. Simulation experiments show that, in finite samples, the
TV-PARX model performs well in terms of model selection and forecasting
accuracy. We also illustrate the empirical usefulness of the time-varying
specification of the proposed TV-PARX model by analyzing the number of new daily
COVID-19 infections in Italy and the number of corporate defaults in the US.
Forecasting algorithms developed within the Autometrics framework are used to
select the best forecasting model for each series. Results show that the
time-varying TV-PARX model is able to capture sudden shifts in the dynamics of
the analyzed time series and often outperforms a set of popular forecasting
models and a static PAR model in forecasting accuracy.

  The Small Inner Detector (SID) of the SiD detector is a silicon vertex and
tracking detector based on a central barrel solenoid magnet with a field of 3.5
T. It consists of two layers of double-layers of eight planes of silicon
barrel layers alternately inclined at $\pm 17^\circ$ and two forward disks
located at the edge of the barrel, divided into 36 forward planes with a
variety of technologies to achieve excellent tracking performance in the
forward regions. The SID design, construction, and integration into the SiD
detector will be presented.
  The SiD Forward ElectroMagnetic (FEM) sections of the calorimeter are
inhabited by the Dual-Field-Gradient Silicon Photodisc (DFGSD), the Silicon
Tungsten Fibre (SWF) and the Highly Granular LAr Proportional Counter (HGIPC)
all designed to achieve excellent energy and position resolution in the
forward regions. The choice of technology for each of the FEM sections was
carefully considered to exploit the strengths of each to meet the performance
requirements for a detector designed for a linear $e^+e-$ collider.
  All of the FEM technologies are segmented into a large number of individual
read out modules, with the HGIPC being a proportional counter with a
highly granular readout, consisting of 2cm x 2cm readout modules, in a
large forward module containing 2000 of these with a total mass of less than
150 kg. The choice of using a Proportional Counter instead of a Time Projection
Chamber (TPC) follows a detailed study comparing the two technologies for this
application. The proposed construction strategy for the HGIPC includes a

has grown to a significant size in the
past years. It makes up to thousands of proofs accessible and usable in a few
clicks. However, many of the proofs written in the past are presented in a
monolithic style which makes them hard to understand and even harder to reuse.
Isabelle proofs are expressed in ML, which is not the easiest language for
reusable components with abstract interfaces. In addition, proofs often
contain unnecessary information, such as user errors, test cases, and
debugging steps.
  To address these issues, we present IDR -- a software development methodology
for proofs, which encourages modular and iterative development with
retroactive testing and reusable intermediate results. IDR marks as "interface"
any piece of proof code which is part of the interface of a module and should
be implemented correctly in order for the module to work correctly. IDR
automatically identifies and register all interfaces implicitly, so that they
are not forgotten. IDR also advocates retroactive testing, i.e., re-running
previous tests on older versions of the codebase whenever the codebase is
updated. In our prototype implementation for Isabelle we put these ideas into
practice by automatically generating and displaying a list of interfaces to be
implemented, along with a list of tests to run, from the development history
and commit messages.
  We demonstrate IDR on a proof of four classic theorems which are well-known
and readily available in the literature of graph theory -- Dirac's theorem,
Ore's theorem, Posa's theorem, and Gallai's theorem. Each of these theorems
depends on previous results from graph theory, which are also proved in
detail following the same structure of interfaces. The development is fully
tuned with IDR's suggestions and it takes around 700 lines of code to cover
over 100,000 lines of code (including 3,000+ theorems from the Isabelle Archive
of Formal Proofs that are required as dependencies). Around half of the code
is marked as interface and around 100 test cases are generated automatically
from commit messages and development history.

variant of eigenvector centrality
for multilayer networks with inter-layer constraints on node importance.
Specifically, we consider a multilayer network defined by multiple
edge-weighted, potentially directed, graphs over the same set of nodes with
each graph representing one layer and no inter-layer edges. As in the case of
standard eigenvector centrality, we want to compute a vector that represents
the importance of each node in each layer and is, up to scaling, fixed under
the mapping defined by the inter-layer constraints and the adjacency matrices
of the individual layers. More formally, such a centrality vector together with
a set of scalar values representing the local importance of the nodes in each
layer would satisfy a system of linear equations involving the adjacency
matrices and the scalar values, as well as a system of linear equations defined
by the centrality vectors in each layer. In this paper, we show how to solve
this system of linear equations efficiently for the centrality vectors and provide a practical algorithm doing so. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm to compute such a
multilayer eigenvector centrality and it has already been implemented in the
NetworkX library.
  Our approach uses a novel reformulation of the problem as a system of linear
equations involving two sets of linear transformations representing the
constraints on node importance in each layer and the mapping defined by the
adjacency matrices of the individual layers. Further, our approach is able to
handle both directed and undirected multilayer networks as well as both
binary and non-binary (weighted) edges in each layer. Finally, our algorithm is
modular and can be customized to fit different use cases and system configurations.
For example, it can be modified to run in restricted memory environments while
still computing the same centrality scores or even to run on distributed
hardware configurations to further improve its performance on very large
multilayer networks.

multilayer networks, both synthetic and real, showing that it is able to
efficiently compute the proposed multilayer eigenvector centrality in various
network settings. Further, we demonstrate the utility of the proposed
multilayer eigenvector centrality by showing how it can be used to capture
node importance in multilayer networks as well as how it can be used in two
different analysis tasks: community detection and link prediction.

differential equality and inequality constraints. Since these problems are
infinite-dimensional and often do not have a known analytical solution, one has
to resort to numerical methods to compute an approximate solution. This paper
focuses on a general class of nonlinear functional optimization problems with
mixed-integer differential algebraic constraints, which encompasses many
individual classes of nonlinear problem classes of interest. A hybrid
architecture that uses model predictive control to provide an efficient
computation of an approximate solution is proposed. The performance of the

  Hybrid procedures for solving online optimal control problems often assume a
nominal trajectory under which the constraints are satisfied. If the actual
state trajectory deviates from the nominal one, the constraints may be violated
and the nominal solution may not be feasible. To account for the uncertainty
in the state trajectory, the control inputs can be tightened up in the online
optimization. However, this may result in a potential loss of feasibility. In
this paper, we propose a robust optimization-based control (ROBC) algorithm,
which guarantees closed-loop constraint satisfaction and suboptimality bounds
for a class of nonlinear control affine systems subject to mixed-integer
infinite-dimensional constraints. The required robustness guarantees are
achieved by utilizing a novel tube-based feedback control policy that takes
into account the uncertainty direction during the optimization. The performance
of the proposed method is illustrated on a ball-and-bowl problem, a car
acceleration problem and a quadcopter flight control problem.

control (ROBC) algorithm, which provides a guaranteed constraint satisfaction

performance of the proposed method is illustrated on a ball-and-bowl problem,

located in complex reservoir formations. To efficiently produce from such
reservoirs, it is often necessary to carry out several injection and production
cycles during the life cycle of an offshore well. To optimize this process and
achieve the highest possible recovery of hydrocarbons from the reservoir, it is
important to plan and schedule the drilling process efficiently. However,
scheduling of drilling and production operations in offshore wells has
received little attention in the literature. In this paper, we present a
mathematical modeling approach for the multi-objective scheduling of drilling
and production operations in offshore wells. The model considers the complex
production technology used for this kind of wells, the wear and tear of the
drill bits, and the maintenance of the well equipment and structure. In
addition, the model accounts for the hydrocarbon recovery from the reservoir
over time and the costs associated with the drilling process, equipment
maintenance, and hydrocarbon sales.
  To solve the scheduling problem, we use a multi-start procedure based on a
partial order reduction technique combined with a population size reduction
strategy, which is made available to the public for the first time in this
paper, called multi-start iterative local search with population size reduction
(MS-ILSRP-SR). The algorithm was implemented in a C++ program and solved using an
Intel Core i7-9700K CPU at 3.80GHz with 32 GB of RAM, using a generic solver
available in CPLEX 12.10 for Windows/x64. The results show that the algorithm
achieves optimal solutions for the medium and large scale problems in a
reasonable computational time, and it is able to explore the Pareto front in
less than one hour for the largest problem considered in this work, which
represents a realistic scenario for an offshore well.

Pareto front solutions for the large scale problem, some practical
recommendations are presented for the offshore industry. In addition, this

authors' knowledge has received little attention in the literature.

model is effective at detecting a wide variety of languages.

classification tasks, where the majority of the text is written in a language
different from the target language. It also provides insights into the

for text classification tasks that use English as the target language. From a
practical perspective, the model is effective at detecting code-mixing in

  Dynamic plan recognition (DRP) is the problem of inferring the sequence of
actions that a person is most likely to have carried out given some observations
of their behavior. Conditional plan recognition adds a twist: the sequence of
actions is likely to have been influenced by a randomly sampled parameter,
while counterfactual plan recognition adds another twist: the sampled parameter
is not random, it is known, but we want to infer what would have been
probabilistically likely had it been random. These three problems can be
combined to address questions of conditional and counterfactual plan recognition
beyond the point of first action, which is how people behave in real life.
$dbss$ can be used to solve these problems and is likely to be orders of
magnitude faster than previously proposed techniques.

amount of intensity inhomogeneity to the input of downstream steps to improve
the intensity similarity to the corresponding non-brain tissues. Our director
network (DN) is trained on a set of ideal brain masks with the addition of
uncertainty maps generated by an ensemble of SSNs. DN further refines the
output of SSN with the guidance of ideal masks and uncertainty maps. The

networks. To investigate this further, we compare the training and testing
performance of two sets of models with different number of training and testing

different modality and performed a different task. This suggests that more

  Our result for SCP measures include subgaussian inequalities of
bounded-difference type extending classical results by Kolmogorov and others.
Such measures can be seen as weak versions of the SRP. In turn, measures
satisfying the full SRP allow us to obtain quantitative concentration of
functions of the form $f(X)+g(Y)$, with $X$ and $Y$ taking values in the
discrete cube and $f$ and $g$ Lipschitz functions on $\mathbb{R}^d$. We also
obtain quantitative concentration results for certain self-intersection
counting functions of random walks on discrete cubes, which in turn imply bounds
on the entropy of the associated Markov chains.

we characterise the strong Rayleigh property (which turns out to be equivalent
to SCP) in terms of bounds on the number of 'bad' pairs of vertices on which
the associated kernel or transition probability decays too slowly. This is
motivated by the weight they carry in quantifying the fourth moment of the
associated transition probabilities (as in the self-intersection
formulas). This regularity property, in turn, allows us to derive improved

1951 thesis by T.A. Springer. In this thesis Springer studied the
classification of conjugacy classes in the symplectic group $Sp_n(K)$, where
the commutative field $K$ is of characteristic different from 2. He finds that
each conjugacy class is characterized by a system of invariants. These
invariants are first of all -- as in the case of the general linear group --
irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers, but -- differently
than in the general linear group -- also maximal totally positive quadratic
forms on $K[x_1,...,x_n]$. Springer also determines the conjugacy classes in the
maximal symplectic group $Sp_{n+1}(K)$ that contains $Sp_n(K)$, and describes
the (group-theoretic) homomorphisms from $Sp_n(K)$ to $Sp_m(K')$, where $K'$ is
a field.

completely natural objects in algebra and Lie theory. It develops the
algebraic and formal technique which would later lead to the presentation of
Bethe ans\"atze in terms of roots of a certain quartic equation, as we found in
an entirely different context with P.R. Kalium and G. van der Hoorn.

the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ in a series of LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$
superlattices as a function of bilayer thickness. Spin-lattice relaxation
measurements in an applied field of 6.55 T reveal two equal amplitude
components: one with metallic ($T$-linear) $1/T_{1}$, and a second with a more
complex $T$-dependence. The metallic character of the slow relaxing component
is only weakly affected by the LaNiO$_3$ thickness, while the fast component is
much more sensitive, exhibiting the opposite temperature dependence (increasing
towards low $T$) in the thinnest, most magnetic samples. The origin of this
bipartite relaxation is discussed.
  We propose that the fast relaxing component may be attributed to a
spectroscopically distinct, but still metallic, region at the interface with a
segregated, ordered nanodomain spin arrangement. The nanodomain hypothesis is
consistent with the strong thickness dependence and suggests that order-by disorder
mechanisms, such as magnetic boundary effects, can stabilize metallic, but
magnetic, nanodomain states in what might otherwise appear to be a
paramagnetic phase.
  Finally, the relative magnitude of the two components changes upon dilution,
increasing in importance at low $T$ for the slow relaxing, metallic component,
and decreasing for the fast component. This change indicates that the slow
component is more sensitive to magnetic ordering.
  The results demonstrate the utility of $\beta$-detected NMR for the study of
correlated metals and magnetically doped oxides and provide detailed information
on the spatial extent of magnetic nanodomain order in metallic
LaNiO$_3$ superlattices.

sentences of written conversational dialog that balances a high branching
factor (10) with several conversation turns (6) through a combination of
algorithmic and human data selection methods. The dialog is written by pairs of
human conversational partners who are given a partially completed conversation
by the proposed algorithm, and are asked to continue the conversation in a
natural but also responsive way, thus curating a path that would not naturally
occur on their own. We show that a model trained on the MultiTalk Dataset to
generate one step at a time outperforms a strong matching model on a variety of
metrics, and when trained to model the likelihood of a whole conversation, it
produces state of the art scores on the Cornell Movie Dialog Corpus and the
MultiTalk Eval Dataset, which we also release. A model that generates one
sentence at a time at the same level of branching performs substantially
worse, highlighting the importance of being able to use several turns of
context.

simultaneously. We propose a task which uses two trained dialog models to
generate a conversation, and evaluates the quality of the resulting
conversation. We also release a set of 2000 conversations, the MultiTalk
Evaluation Dataset, which is particularly designed to evaluate the quality of
multi-part dialog.

and their corresponding bifurcations, in a given model by only using its
nonlinear stability properties. Our approach is based on the notion that in a
parameter space, bifurcations typically occur at the boundary between two
regions with different dynamical states. Therefore, if a system undergoes a
bifurcation at a parameter value $r^*$, its energy (or nonlinear stability
properties) will present a discontinuity when approaching $r^*$ from both
sides. To identify such points we use a model-independent metric, the
r\'nyi-bifurcation entropy, which quantifies the local degree of discontinuity
of the energy with respect to the parameter. We numerically showed that this
approach is able to identify all bifurcations, including those leading to
complex states, in several nonlinear systems and also analytically proved its
ability to identify the bifurcation leading to the onset of chaos in the
Zebrafish model. Moreover, by using a set of randomly chosen initial conditions
we showed that the present approach is also able to identify several unstable
states, including those with complex dynamics. In order to fully understand its
performance, we also developed a mock-up procedure to follow the track of a
single state in the configuration space of a system. By comparing the results
obtained with and without noise, we showed that our approach is capable to
identify not only stable but also unstable states, even when the dynamical
trajectories are highly damped by noise.
  Finally, by using a statistical analysis, we showed that the number of
identifiable states increases with the total number of trajectories used to
compute the r\'nyi-bifurcation entropy. In conclusion, in this work we
introduced the r\'nyi-bifurcation entropy, a robust model-independent metric,
to identify several types of bifurcations and unstable states in complex
dynamical systems.

we propose a lightweight hardware monitor that can detect the presence of
performance degradation on a microarchitecture, and guide a user towards a

detected performance degradation, the monitor can indicate the presence of

privacy-preserving learning paradigm that allows
multiple parities to jointly train a powerful machine learning model without
sharing their private data. According to the form of collaboration, FL can be
further divided into horizontal federated learning (HFL) and vertical federated
learning (VFL). In HFL, participants share the same feature space and
collaborate on the same sample space, while in VFL, participants share the same
sample space but collaborate on different feature spaces. VFL has a broader
application scenario and more potential collaboration partners, but it often
involits non-trivial challenges such as data alignment and private model
aggregation. In this paper, we focus on VFL and summarize its main challenges,
existing solutions, and future directions.
  According to the activation format of the local model parameters, the
activation format of the intermediate product, and the private participation
scheme, we categorize the existing VFL solutions into three categories:
logistic-based, linear-based, and private protocol-based, and summarize their
advantages and disadvantages. Finally, we discuss the potential solutions to the
existing challenges and propose a general framework for VFL. The framework
includes two key components: the activation format conversion and the private
model aggregation. Our framework and solutions demonstrate that VFL provides a
more flexible and private way to collaborate than conventional methods and has
great potential to be applied in a variety of applications, such as
multi-institution analysis of medical image datasets and collaborative
recommendation systems. The VFL framework and solutions also show that careful
design of data alignment schemes and private model aggregation methods is
important to achieve efficient and secure collaboration in VFL.

valve replacement
surgery in patients with the congenital heart disease Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)
is challenging. In the growing organs, the extracellular matrix provides a
compliant and potentially informative medium for the mechanical tracts of the
blood vessels. The stiffening of this matrix due to fibrosis alters the
immaterial response to haemodynamics. The impact of these changes on the flow
patterns remains to be investigated. Here, we study the impact of the
stiffening of the pulmonary arteries in the setting of haemodynamic loads
induced by the native or transplanted main pulmonary artery in a 3D
multi-physics model of the TOF circulation. We show that the stiffening of the
pulmonary arteries significantly alters the haemodynamic loads on the distal
branches and leads to the development of haemodynamic hotspots in the
post-operative configuration. These results may contribute to the planning of
the optimal time of intervention for pulmonary valve replacement surgery in
patients with TOF and may provide new mechanistic insights into the development
of pulmonary artery fibrosis following pulmonary valve replacement.
  The present model assumes a rigid extracellular matrix, which is not
realistic for children. For future work, non-linear viscoelastic models of the
extracellular matrix would be integrated into the model to further investigate
the impact of haemodynamics on fibrosis and the effect of fibrosis on
haemodynamics.

behavior of a random uniform parking
function $\pi_n$ on the set of permutations of length $n$ having no ascending
sequences of length $4$ called the 1342-avoiding permutations. We show that the
first seven letters of $\pi_n$, i.e. the first seven elements in the parking
lot, are asymptotically determined deterministically, and provide explicit
limits. As a consequence, the first seven letters of $\pi_n$ have the same
asymptotic behavior as the first seven elements in the parking lot, i.e., the
determinantal parking field with the hard-core constraint being studied in the
electrical and statistical physics communities. Our proof uses the recursive
formula for the 1342-avoiding permutations and is purely combinatorial.
  Moreover, we conjecture that the next three letters, i.e., the eighth, ninth
and tenth letters of $\pi_n$, are asymptotically determined randomly, and
provide explicit probabilities. It is interesting to note that the hard-core
parking field is determined deterministically while the soft-core parking
field is given by the Thouless--Bedjoson process and is asymptotically random.
The soft-core parking field and the hard-core parking field behave differently
likely due to the presence of an inverse temperature in the energy minimization
process of the soft-core parking field but not in the hard-core case.
  To support our conjecture, we show that the normalized sum of the first nine
elements in $\pi_n$ has the same asymptotic behavior as a random variable
studied by Aldous, and provide an explicit limit.

information and energy at the receiver are considered and the optimization
objective is maximum distance between these two areas. The integer on/off
status of the transmitter and the binary switchable transfer efficiency at the
receiver are considered as parameters in the resource allocation. The
entitlement of the receiver to adjust the relative power at the two separate
areas in order to satisfy the power requirement is introduced in the resource
allocation. The resource optimization is performed in an information-theoretic
sense, where the transmit rate at the transmitter is used as the metric to
achieve the maximum distance between the two areas at the receiver. A
formulation of a non-convex optimization problem is first presented, then the
dismantling of the problem into three sub-problems is presented in order to
apply convex optimization tools to find the solution. The proposed resource
allocation presents novel distance measures between the two areas at the
receiver, and it provides expressivity to the transfer efficiency at the
receiver, in addition to allowing on/off transmission status at the transmitter.

communication and energy demands at the receiver, while maximizing the distance
between the two separate areas.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD). In
language, words of the same form can take different meanings and understanding
the context to determine the meaning can be a challenging but human like task.
For this study, we design and implement a curriculum learning based approach
to train a BERT based model for WSD. We use a set of words from the standard
benchmark dataset, Leon, and create a dataset of about 300K examples. We
demontstrate that our approach is able to achieve an average F-score of 38 on
the test data which is an improvement over the current state-of-the-art. We
also observe that our model is able to learn the meaning of words from the
dataset and generalize to other words of similar context.
  Curriculum learning has been shown to work for many tasks. But for this
particular task, interestingly we observe that the optimal learning curve is
not a monotonically changing hyperplane but rather a complex curve which also
changes along multiple dimensions. To handle this complexity we use a
multi-dimensional curriculum and observe nice improvements on the test data.
Also, observing the human WSD skills we try to simplify the task by removing
the noise of multiple senses for a single word and create a sub-task of
distinguishing two senses of a word, called Dual WSD or DWSD. We observe nice
improvements on the test data for DWSD and also observe that our model is
able to generalize to other words of similar context.
  To understand the complexity of the learning curve of WSD we try to simplify
the task by changing the ontology and creating a sub-task of Single WSD or
SWSD. We observe interesting learning curve patterns for different changes in
ontology and also observe nice improvements on the test data for SWSD.
Interestingly we observe that the ontology used by Gibson et al. [1] is the
optimal one and any change in the ontology does not improve but rather
degrades the score on the test data.

and also try to super-vise the development of sense inventory by creating a
sub-task of Dual WSD or DWSD. We also try to understand the complexity of the
learning curve of WSD by analyzing different aspects of the standard
benchmark dataset, Leon.

language understanding tasks such as coreference resolution, it is very
challenging to obtain explicit supervision for sequentialization, particularly
for large-scale language understanding tasks that require inferring event
structures from massive amounts of text. In this work, we propose a self-
supervised pretraining strategy to learn encoding functions that can
appropriately sequence unordered events. We use the coreference resolution task
as a "teacher" to do self-supervised training. The key insight is that once the
coreference resolution task has been used to obtain representations of two
entities, it is feasible to obtain the implicit supervision for sequentialize
the two entities by comparing the representation of representation-comparison
data. We apply the proposed self-supervised pretraining strategy to pretrain a
language understanding model on the Wikipedia dataset and evaluate it on the
Coref-QA and Coref-Gen datasets. Experimental results show that the proposed
self-supervised pretraining strategy improves the sequentialization ability of
the model without using explicit supervision on unordered event sequences.
Furthermore, we find that inferences made on Wikipedia can generalize to
coreference resolution and zero-shot semantic generation tasks beyond the
application domain.
  We study the task of sequentializing unordered entities, i.e., automatically
determining the linear order of entities given the entities themselves. While
considerable progress has been made in coreference resolution, the coref task
has much overlap with sequentialization, e.g., both involve resolving
proximity-based ambiguities. However, existing datasets for sequentialization
are small-scale and targeted at specific domains or applications. Here, we study
sequentialization from a language understanding perspective using the Coref
dataset. We find that even without using explicit supervision on entity
sequences, coreference resolution alone can well handle many sequentialization
cases. To further improve sequential understanding, we propose to leverage the
best practices in coreference resolution, including multi-task learning with
neural models and adversarial training with generative models. Experimental
results show that these coreference-specific improvements are crucial to
sequentialization. Codes and datasets are released at

we analyze and solve an inverse problem of a dynamic network which is
represented by a time-varying graph. Specifically, we want to find the maximum
damage to the network by changing some of its adjacency elements (i.e.,
changing some of the connections or changing some of the entry types of the
connection matrix) at a given time $k$ (i.e., $A_k \to A_{k+1}$ with
$\tau=1$). This problem is represented by a discrete dynamical system defined
by a graph (Decision Graph of Degree one) and we find that the solution is a
periodic binary sequence. When the period is equal to the length of the orbit
we also find the initial and final states of the sequence. In the case of an
arbitrarily long period we present a rule in order to get the next term of the
sequence. We also present some applications such as the Clube's model of the
Solar System, the Euler's Four-Body Problem, and the problem of the
dissolution of a network.

We demonstrate an all-optical method to measure the spin-exchange relaxation of
collided pairs (SERP) collision rate in a rubidium vapor. The method is based on
the fact that the SERP collision rate is proportional to the number of
collisions between spin-polarized atoms. In our setup, an optical beam is split
into two counter-propagating beams that intersect at a right angle. One of the
beams is first absorbed by a cloud of antiparallel spins and then reflected of
a mirror to intersect with the other beam. The absorption by the antiparallel
spin causes a phase shift in the reflected beam only when the atoms are
polarized in the $\left| F=1, m_{F}=0\right>$ state. The phase shift is
measured by using a Mach-Zender interferometer. By adjusting the optical
properties of the setup, the measured phase shift is shown to be directly
proportional to the SERP collision rate. We also show that the main limitations
of the method can be used in a laser-ablation-based exoplanet detection
technique to improve the detectability of a exoplanet in cases when the
exoplanet is mostly in the Doppler shift.

optimal power allocation (PA) for a downlink (DL) XL-MIMO system serving $K$
single-antenna users (UAs) with a large-scale MIMO transmitter (LTx). First, we
express the DL performance in terms of sum-rate (SR) as a function of the Tx
correlation matrix and the power allocation vector. Second, we formulate an
optimization problem aiming to maximize the SR, subject to the total power
budget constraint and the non-negative power allocation elements. Third, by
utilizing the alternating optimization technique and matrix factorization, we
propose an efficient power allocation algorithm with the optimal solution for the
correlated XL-MIMO scenario. Numerically simulated results verify the proposed
solution's accuracy and show significant SR improvement, up to $2.5$ times
higher values, in some cases. The proposed solution shows promising performance

of disks surrounding young stars have shown that their morphology is made of
azimuthally-symmetric or point-symmetric substructures, in some cases with
spiral arms. The location and characteristics of these substructures are
dependent on the distance to the host star. The origin of the substructures is
still debated. We form spirals in hydrodynamically unstable regions, far from
the star, by the self-installation of spirals in a parameter-free way. We show
that the substructures observed in the protoplanetary disk surrounding SAO 206
108 reported by Fujii et al. (2020) can be explained by the density
perturbations created by the hydrodynamical instability in the spirit of our
previous studies. Unlike previous studies that focus on the analysis of
observations of disks with spirals only, here we follow the evolution of the
disk from the formation of the spirals to the outer regions. We show that the
inner spirals are extensions of the hydrodynamical spirals, in a region where
the density perturbations have been amplified by the accumulation of mass
streaming through the inner regions. Different from the hydrodynamical
substructures, the inner substructures in Fujii et al. (2020) have spiral arms
with a large opening angle, which are formed by the direct motion of accreting
protoplanets.
  We also discuss how our model can be extended to explain the rings reported
in the disk. By assuming that the protoplanets responsible for the substructures
are massless, we show that if the density perturbations are stronger than a
critical value, the density inside the spirals drops to create a ring-like
structure in the disk.

developed in the disks to connect the substructures to planetary systems.

spirals-and-rings sequence, are formed dominantly by the hydrodynamical
instability, and that the inner point-like substructures are extensions of the
hydrodynamical ones to the inner regions.

interferometric fringe pattern of counter propagating equal and opposite
symmetric beams of the Sagnac interferometer whether it is on the Earth or on
the moon. Thus, calling it a gyroscopes for this purpose is not correct. A
gyroscope is an device which is used to measure the angular momentum of a system
and this can be done with the help of a gyroscopic Sagnac interferometer by
introducing a small transverse motion to the otherwise counter propagating
symmetric beams. The fringe pattern of this interferometer depends on the
transverse Doppler shift of the moving interferometer mirror along with the
Sagnac effect. The transverse Doppler shift further depends on the longitudinal
Doppler shift of the counter propagating beams. The longitudinal Doppler shift
arises due to the relative motion along the line of sight producing equal but
opposite frequency shifts on the two counter propagating beams. The equal but
opposite frequency shifts result in the self interference phenomenon or the
spectral anomaly around the interferometer's fringe center. The longitudinal

counter propagating beams are exactly at the line of sight i.e. when the beam

based on FPGAs or ASICs, model parallelism is a promising strategy, as it
provides an effective way to increase the effective model size by utilizing
multiple processing units. However, existing communication protocols based on
all-gather are not efficient for large models due to the large number of

model. In this work, we propose a novel communication protocol for model
parallelism called WaveAllGather. The key idea is to perform an all-gather
operation in a wave-like manner, where each processing unit first communicates
with its neighboring units in a wave direction and then in the other direction.

communication protocol.

WaveAllGather and evaluate it using a simulator. The source code of the
simulator is available online.

energy consumption for various applications. For model parallelism with 16
processing units, WaveAllGather achieves an average communication latency of

protocol, and an average energy consumption of 0.033$pJ/ bit$, which is
1.18$\times$ lower than the baseline. For sharded parallelism with 16
processing units, WaveAllGather achieves an average communication latency of

is a critical area in the treatment of
infectious diseases. An NPR is designed to prevent the dissemination of
pathogens from inside the room to the outside. An NPR typically requires both
physical and operational design measures. The physical design measures include
creation of a pressure gradient between adjacent rooms by controlling the
infiltration rates through the intermediate rooms, selection of the appropriate
fans and control systems, and proper sealing of the room. The operational design
measure includes continuous monitoring of pressure gradients between adjacent
rooms during the normal and emergency operating conditions. During an emergency
operation, the NPR may require additional design measures such as isolation of
the fan systems and provision of ventilation air to the NPR. The pressure
 gradients during NPR operations are influenced by several parameters including
infiltration rates through intermediate rooms, fan flow rates, duct friction
losses, fan total pressure, and isolation of fan systems. Although the
influencing parameters are well known, there is no systematic approach available
in the literature to design and operable conditions of NPRs. In this paper, I
develop a novel methodology to design and monitor NPRs during normal and emergency
operating conditions. The methodology provides a framework to calculate
pressure gradients between NPR and adjacent rooms during normal and emergency
operations and provides guidelines for selection of fans and design of fan
control systems. The novelty of the methodology lies in the fact that it
incorporates the effect of duct friction losses in design and operation of NPRs
and provides a framework to monitor NPRs. The methodology is general in nature
and can be applied to design and monitor any NPR in the world.
  From Sep 2020 to Feb 2022, the pressure gradients in 12 NPRs were monitored as
part of the COVID-19 operations. During this period, the pressure gradients
remained within design specifications in 10 NPRs. However, two NPRs had
continuously violated the design specifications. The violating conditions were
captured by the methodology developed in this paper and the reasons behind the
violations were investigated. The investigation showed that the design
specifications were not met during the commissioning phase of the two NPRs. The
remedial measures were taken after investigation and the pressure gradients in
the two NPRs were brought within design specifications. This shows that the
methodology developed in this paper is practical and can be used to monitor and
improve the operations of NPRs.

of firming in low-carbon grids. A
common concern raised for storage in dispatch is its ability to provide
upstream visibility of its generation and consumption schedules. This concern
is often tied to questions about the reliability of storage to supply firm
capacity. While storage has been shown to provide both spinning and non-spinning
firm capacity, the amount is often quantified and valued differently than
traditional generation resources. To date, storage in reliability assessments
has been modeled primarily as a reserve resource. However, this paper shows
that such an approach underestimates the amount of firming that storage can
provide. A more accurate representation of the firming provided by storage can
lead to a re-examination of its economics in dispatch and can inform procurement
policies for capacity markets and long-term contracts.
  In this paper, we use a unit commitment model to quantify the spinning and
non-spinning firm capacity of storage in different low-carbon futures. We then
compare the amount of firm capacity provided by storage to traditional
generation resources. Finally, we value the firm capacity and reserves provided
by storage using a simple capacity market design and compare the resulting
revenue to the operating costs of the resources. Our results show that storage
can provide significantly more firm capacity than previously quantified in the
literature and that this firm capacity is valued highly in capacity markets.
However, the revenue from capacity markets may not be enough to cover the costs
of storage in some scenarios. Reliability standards and capacity markets will
need to be designed carefully to incentivize the investment and operation of
resources that can provide firm capacity across a range of low-carbon futures.
The value of firm capacity will only be fully realized if it is explicitly
included in capacity market designs.

the process of selecting the most informative samples and training a classifier
with annotated samples is interwoven. As a result, the performance of active
learning depends on both sample selection and classifier training. While
tremendous efforts have been made to improve sample selection, little work has
been done to evaluate and compare AL algorithms, due to the following issues:
lack of standardized benchmarks and reproducibility issues in AL evaluation.
To address these issues, ActiveLearn is proposed, a Python library for evaluating
and comparing AL algorithms. The library provides a set of standardized
benchmarks, and is designed with modular structure to make it scalable for
evaluating AL algorithms on various datasets and scenarios. ActiveLearn is
released under the MIT License, and available at
https://github.com/ChangXuTeng/ActiveLearn. With ActiveLearn, researchers can
easily compare and evaluate the performance of AL algorithms, and also develop
new AL algorithms and algorithms for classifier training and sample selection,
making it a comprehensive active learning library.
  ActiveLearn is composed of three main modules: data, algorithms, and tools.
ActiveLearn.Data provides a set of standardized benchmarks, including image,
text, and audio classification datasets, as well as meta-learning benchmarks.
ActiveLearn.Algorithms contains a variety of AL algorithms, including random
sampling, uncertainty sampling, and evolutionary strategy, and allows users to
easily implement and compare their own AL algorithms. ActiveLearn.Tools contains
tools for evaluating AL algorithms, including metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1 score)
and curves (e.g., learning curves), as well well-established AL evaluation
protocols (e.g., reservoir sampling). ActiveLearn is designed with modular
structure to make it scalable for handling different data types and learning
tasks. For example, image classification and meta-learning share the same
sampling algorithms, but with different performance metrics.
  The main contributions of ActiveLearn are (1) a set of standardized learning
benchmarks, (2) a modular design for handling different data types and learning
tasks, and (3) a fully open-sourced library with which researchers can easily
compare and evaluate the performance of AL algorithms. With ActiveLearn, AL
research can be more efficient, reproducible, and accurate, ultimately
contributing to building more intelligent and reliable AI systems.

considerable progress in this area in the past years, measuring and comparing
the effectiveness of fuzzers is still an open research question. In software
testing, the gold standard for evaluating test quality is mutation analysis,
assessing the ability of a test to detect synthetic bugs; if a set of tests
fails to detect such mutations, it will also fail to detect real bugs. Mutation
analysis, however, is too expensive for large and complex programs. A more
practical, but still scientifically sound, criterion is to correlate with
mutation analysis: that is, tests that score well on mutations should also be
able to detect real bugs. With this criterion in mind, we introduce mutation
adapters, specialized mutations that capture real behavior deviations; and we
introduce a new simple and efficient methodology to evaluate and compare fuzz
tools that leverages mutation analysis; thereby allowing safe and scientifically
sound comparisons of fuzz tools.
  To validate our methodology, we adapted it to evaluate five popular fuzzing
tools on two binaries and found a clear correlation between the number of
mutations that each fuzzer can detect and the number of real bugs that the
fuzzers are able to trigger; and we were able to reproduce known results
previously obtained on one of the tested binaries; and discover new
vulnerabilities; including a critical vulnerability in the OpenSSL library
that we did not see despite trying hard; further confirming the effectiveness
of this methodology.
  We release our mutation adapter framework, including all engineering
guidelines, and the data we collected during this project to encourage and
facilitate future research in this area.
  In particular, we want to encourage the creation of a mutation repository
that fuzz tools can draw from, and a set of guidelines for the adaptation of
mutations to new programs and languages.
  Finally, we propose a set of programs and languages for which we were unable
to adapt mutations (e.g., Python, JavaScript) and which could help further
validate the usefulness of this framework.
  In summary, in this work we present a new methodology for evaluating and
comparing fuzzing tools that leverages mutation analysis; we release a
framework that includes a set of engineering guidelines for the mutation
adapters; and we validate the methodology with a set of experiments on two
binaries.

verify that some of them can detect real bugs.

$\lambda$-Lipschitz games in which every player's payoff function is
$\lambda$-Lipschitz with respect to the actions of the other players. They
showed that such games admit $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria for
certain settings of $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$. They left open, however, the
question of how hard it is to find such an equilibrium. In this work, we
develop a query-efficient reduction from more general games to Lipschitz games.
We use this reduction to show a query lower bound for any randomized algorithm
finding $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria of $n$-player,
binary-action, $\lambda$-Lipschitz games that is exponential in
$\frac{n\lambda}{\epsilon}$. In addition, we introduce ``multi-Lipschitz
games,'' a generalization that combines multiple such games, and show that any
randomized algorithm finding an $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria
must query exponential in $\frac{n(\lambda_1+\ldots+\lambda_k)}{\epsilon}$,
where $n$ is the number of players and $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k$ are the
Lipschitz parameters controlled by the players.

$\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibrium with probability at least $1/4$.

modification of the ``cut" analysis of even-Dar and Shieferman [EC'19] and
our own refinement of the "mix" analysis of Yi-Jiun Su and Changbin Yu
[EC'20]. The reduction finds a complex ``template'' that contains several
``doors'' that an algorithm must pass through to find an approximate equilibrium. The analysis then shows that any algorithm must query at least as many "doors" to find such an equilibrium.

performance of machine learning models, allowing model selection and parameter
tuning. However, the very process of CV introduces random variation, and
different folds will give different estimates of performance. It is common
practice to average the performance across all folds, but this averaging
effectively ignores the extra variation introduced by the CV. Here, we show how
to properly account for this extra variation, obtaining a proper posterior
distribution over model performance that can be used for Bayesian model
selection and parameter tuning. We demonstrate our method on a simulated and
two real datasets, showing that it can provide posterior credible interval
estimates of performance that are significantly narrower than those obtained by
averaging across folds. Our method provides a way to estimate model
performance that is more accurate and reliable than traditional CV.
Furthermore, it provides a way to compare different models in an unbiased
manner, effectively controlling for the variation introduced by CV. We show that
by accounting for this variation, we can obtain posterior estimates of the
relative performance of different models that are free from bias.

returning results that are in line with our prior knowledge of the system
underneath.

transitions in their flow behavior when sheared at high stresses. Such
transitions occur when the dominant interactions between the suspended
particles shift from hydrodynamic to frictional. Here, we use drag on a cloud
of bouncing gel particles through drag on a cloud of stickering polymer particles
as models and discover that these two transitions are structurally similar.
Despite the large difference in the strength and persistence of the individual
particle interactions, the two transitions occur at roughly the same relative
stress, and have similar values of shear rate times radius times viscosity.
Furthermore, both transitions are marked by a sudden increase in the normalized
viscosity as well as a decrease in the degree of particle orientation. These
results suggest that there is a universal threshold interaction force above which
frictional interactions dominate the behavior of the particles and that
further work should be done to understand why the bouncing particles undergo a
much more dramatic transition than do the stickering polymer particles.
Finally, our findings have implications for the design of future sheared
dispersions that target the engineering of sharp transitions for the purpose of
drag or stress in high-shear applications.
  The critical interaction force marks the transition from hydrodynamic to
frictional inispersions, but its magnitude is not well understood. Here, we
examine this question in three different thickening dispersions: one composed of
polymer particles that stick to each other in shear flow and undergo frictional
interactions, one composed of gel particles that bounce off of each other in
fluid flow and undergo hydrodynamic interactions, and one composed of
polymer-coated gel particles that have both frictional and hydrodynamic
interactions. Using drag on these dispersions as a function of shear stress as
our metric, we find that the critical interaction force in the stickler and
bouncer dispersions is approximately equal to the hydrodynamic force acting on a
single particle in shear flow. Furthermore, we find that the drag in the
bicomponent dispersions can be accurately predicted by simply summing the drag
due to the frictional and hydrodynamic interactions separately. This suggests
that the critical interaction force in these thickening dispersions marks the
transition from hydrodynamic to frictional interactions, and that the sum of the
hydrodynamic and frictional forces is approximately equal to this critical

professional knowledge work is
an understudied area. Here we investigate how public administration
specialists search for and find official government information on the Web.
Public administration specialists are expected to adhere to formal procedures
when searching and finding official information, such as following approved
search procedures and verifying information through multiple sources. While
official government information is readily available on the Web, its discovery
is often difficult due to the lack of clear indicators of authoritativeness and
relevance in search engine results. In addition, search engines and online
services often use personalisation to influence the search experience,
potentially bypassing approved search procedures. We conduct an experimental
field study with ten public administration specialists, where subjects are
given real-world tasks that require finding official information on the Web.
Half of the subjects use a search engine with personalisation enabled, while the
other half uses a search engine with personalisation disabled. We compare the
 effectiveness of both search conditions in finding official information,
verifying information through multiple sources, and adhering to approved search
procedures. We find that search personalisation significantly degrades the
performance of human experts searching for official information. When searching
with personalisation, subjects more often need to use multiple searches to find
the information, and more often fail to find official information altogether.
Also, search personalisation reduces the adherence to approved search procedures.
We further find that even though search engines without personalisation return
older results, they are more likely to be verified through multiple sources.
Subjective feedback also indicates that search personalisation increases the
perceived relevance of results at the expense of authoritativeness. We conclude
that Web search personalisation can compromise the effectiveness and
reliability of human experts in finding official information on the Web, which
is critical for many professional knowledge work tasks.
  We discuss the implications of this study for search engine design,
online services for public administration, and Web search from a human expert
perspective. We propose future research directions for further investigating the
impact of search personalisation on human experts searching for official
information.

  Methods: A novel respiratory compensated 4D $T_2$-weighted (i.e.,
susceptibility-compensated) turbo spin echo sequence was developed on a 1.5 T
MRI scanner for evaluation. The sequence features a susceptibility compensation
gradient (SCG) in combination with respiratory gated 3D k-space encoding and
respiratory navigated 2D k-space encoding for compensation of respiratory
motions. The imaging geometry was designed to match that of a standard 4D
sequences currently used in clinical environment. The performance of the
sequence was evaluated in phantom and in five healthy volunteers who underwent
free-breathing 4D data acquisitions with both this sequence and a currently
used 4D $T_2$-weighted spiral sequence. Reconstruction of the data from this
study employed a proprietary 4D reconstruction algorithm, and image quality was
evaluated visually and quantitatively by means of regional k-space
propagation-based (RKP-based) metrics. In addition, tumor delineation was
evaluated using two different clinical 4D segmentation protocols.
  Results: The RKP-based metrics indicated that the proposed sequence
outperformed the spiral sequence in terms of lateral motion and eddy current
artefacts. Visual evaluation of the images acquired with the proposed sequence
revealed fewer artefacts compared to the spiral sequence. Furthermore,
delimitation of tumors with the proposed sequence compared to the spiral
sequence showed agreement with the ground truth in two of five volunteers.
Conclusion: The proposed 4D $T_2$-weighted turbo spin echo sequence is
suitable for 4D tumor delineation and offers lower artefacts compared to a
corresponding spiral sequence.

tumors in the head and neck, prostate, and lung regions prior to radiation
therapy and compare the delineations obtained with the proposed sequence to
those obtained with currently used 4D spiral sequences.

identify that people often assume the test statistics are independent despite

interpretation of the $p$-values when the test statistics are strongly

algorithms to perform the permutation test when the test statistics are
dependent. For example, it can take weeks to complete an experiment with 8
models and 10 datasets in practice. We propose to use symmetric rank-based
summary statistics to reduce the computational cost while maintaining
efficiency. Moreover, we can further simplify the algorithm by drawing random
permutations without replacement, which further speeds up the experiment by

79 developed economies from 2001
to 2016, with detailed information on energy consumption structures,
environmental regulations, international trade, and R\&D investments. Using
quantitative and qualitative methods, we find that developed economies have
shifted towards cleaner energy consumption structure, but at a very slow pace
(-0.16% per year over 2001-2016), which is not commensurate with the urgent
needs to combat global climate change and achieve sustainable development.
Moreover, we find strong evidence of environmental Kuznets curve (EKC) with a
global (developed and developing economies combined) turning point of $47,939 in
2016 dollars. However, if we estimate the model only for the developed economies,
we find no significant turning point in energy emissions, indicating that the
global turning point is mainly driven by the changes in energy consumption
structures in developing economies. Finally, our regression analysis shows that
environmental policies, international trade, and R\&D investments have
significant impacts on energy emissions in the global sample as well as in the
sample of developed economies.
  From policy perspectives, our findings suggest that developed economies need
to accelerate their transition towards cleaner energy consumption structures
and also strengthen international cooperation with other economies to achieve
global climate goals. Our findings also suggest that environmental policies,
international trade, and R\&D investments can help in reducing energy emissions
and may be used as policy instruments by governments of developed economies.
Moreover, since the global (developed and developing economies combined)
emissions path is already on track to exceed the target of limiting global
warming to less than 1.5$^{\circ}$C above the pre-industrial level, it is
imperative for policymakers to adopt more stringent policies to mitigate the
adverse impacts of climate change and achieve sustainable development.
  Finally, it is also important for future research to use new innovative
methods and techniques to estimate the global and regional turning points in
energy emissions and explore the relationships between energy consumption
structures, environmental policies, international trade, R\&D investments, and
economic growth and income.

Several companies now-a-days provide services and tools to analyze the stock
market and provide better investment decisions. These companies make predictions
of stock prices by collecting historical data of the stocks from various sources
and by applying machine learning algorithms on this data. Although the
performance of such tools and applications can be high, it is not the best
because the quality of the training data can affect the performance of the
machine learning model. Although there are reliable sources from which the
required data can be collected, these sources may charge a lot of money for
providing services or may have a lot of delay in providing the data. To make
tools and applications providing stock market analysis more reliable and widely
available, it is necessary to have a default dataset for training and testing
the models which includes all the required information about the stock market.
This note provides a dataset for the stock market which includes information
about stock issues in Indian stock market along with daily price movement of
each stock for the year 2020. This dataset can be used to train and test
machine learning models with Indian stock market data.
  The dataset contains information about 5078 stocks with their International
Securitisation Agreements Identifier, Stock Issuer Name, Stock Issuer Code,
Industry, Sector, Stock Issued Date, Stock Listing Date, Stock Type, Stock
Status, Board of Security, Open Price, High Price, Low Price, Prevoius Day
Close Price, Closed Price, Volume, and Turnover. This dataset can be used to
train and test machine learning models with Indian stock market data. The
performance of the model was tested by training a simple Random Forest model
with 70% of the data and testing it on the remaining 30% of the data. The
model was found to be correct in predicting the price movement of the stock
market for 80% of the test data.

hand-crafted heuristics and are limited in modeling diversity. Our goal is to
model the underlying distribution of traffic scenes so that actors can be
generated to follow the same distribution. To achieve this, we propose a
differentiable actor generation model (AGM) that encodes a bi-directional
long short-term memory (LSTM) network and a multi-scale rendering module (MRM)
into one end-to-end differentiable network. The AGM predicts a hidden
representation of the scene encoded by the LSTM and reconstructs the scene by
sampling actors following the predicted representation with the MRM. To
optimization AGM, we propose to use a discriminator with multiple scales to
encode the complex underlying distribution of the training dataset, which is
generated by real-world driving behavior, into a set of discriminative features.

actors to follow the same distribution. We evaluate the proposed method
sensitively with CarND dataset and real-world driving behavior from National
Highway Traffic Simulation Analysis System (NHTSSA) and get promising results.

time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) is the ability to preserve
certain properties of the continuum solution, such as conservation laws and
dissipation structures. In this work, we leverage the fact that many
$\mathcal{N}$-width based methods, such as artificial neural networks and
polynomial chaos expansions, already possess some of these properties and aim to
develop a general framework which enables the identification and transfer of
these representations across continuum manifolds. This is achieved through the
introduction of a continuum atlas which describes a family of compatible
manifolds, via a collection of parametrizing maps and their corresponding
tangent map representations. Subsequently, we define the notion of a
\textit{atlas-consistent} estimator which utilizes the atlas to estimate the
$\mathcal{N}$-width of the approximation error on each manifold, resulting in a
family of error bounds which are directly linked to the parametrizing maps. As
a demonstration of the utility of this framework, we use the atlas to construct
atlas-consistent estimators for a class of linear PDEs with time-dependent
dynamical domains. The use of an atlas allows for the incorporation of
\textit{geometric} information about the evolving domain into the estimators,
resulting in error bounds which are shown to be more accurate compared to
non-atlas-consistent estimators.
  Finally, we note that while the focus of this work is centered on PDEs, the
notion of an atlas could be extended to other continuum models, such as those
described by differential algebraic equations or dynamical systems, to name a
few.
  The accompanying code package contains a Python package called
atlas_pde which contains classes for representing the parametrizing maps,
tangent map representations, and estimators for estimating the $\mathcal{N}$-width
of the approximation error. Additionally, the package contains a JAX package
calledjax_atlas which contains functions for constructing atlas-consistent
estimators and examples of how to use them to estimate the error for a few
examples of time-dependent linear PDEs.
  Future work will center around extending the framework to time-dependent
atlas and incorporating higher-order approximations such as rational chaos
expansions.

hole (SBH) binaries (BHB) in the centre of early galaxies, which include a
central dust cloud. We investigate the effect of the dust on the merger of the
BHB. In most cases the dust is ejected from the galaxy by the BHB as it evolves
through the galaxy. However, in a number of cases the dust remains in place
and is deformed as the BHB moves back and forth. Although the deformation is
small, it is sufficient in some cases to prevent the merger for a very long
period, in one case by more than a factor of 10. This is because the drag
force becomes linear with velocity as it moves beyond the dust ring, whereas it
was previously supralinear so that the BHB was merging.

higher and hotter regions of the galaxy. This leads to further interesting
phenomena, such as cooling by line emission and possible grain growth and
agglomeration into dust clouds. In some cases the BHB is merged by a giant
molecular cloud.

presented are not sufficient to prevent BHB merger. In this case the radial
motion of the BHB is by far the most important for determining the merger time.

anisotropic. Although the BHB is always by far the most massive in our models
and the dust dynamics are deterministic we term this a possible route to
formation of internal stellar perturbers in future generations of stars.

the dust may become bound to the galaxy by the gravitational force from the
baryons before the BHB merger is complete.

3D detection (Far3Det) of objects beyond a
certain distance from an observer, e.g., $>$50m. Far3Det is particularly
important for autonomous vehicles (AVs) operating at highway speeds, which
require detections of far-field obstacles to ensure sufficient braking
distances. However, contemporary AV benchmarks such as NuScenes and
KITTRIGHT do not provide far far-field 3D annotations, instead truncating at
distances between 30-50m. To evaluate Far3Det algorithms, we present
HighwayScenes (HS): a new open-mixed dataset recorded in a ten-mile stretch of
highway near Los Angeles. Recorded using a rigid mount of cameras and sensors
on a moving vehicle, HighwayScenes includes 120 clips of 3D 3D reconstructions
of scenes centered around roadways. We apply a set of metrics that account for
the tradeoffs between precision, recall, and distance, introducing the
Far3Det metric which will be made available as an open-source Python package.
Our analysis reveals that contemporary Far3Det algorithms are able to detect
only about half of the far-field (50-80m) objects present in validation
meters. We show that by training on our dataset, contemporary models are able
to significantly improve Far3Det performance. We also show that a simple
curvature regularizer module (CRM) significantly improves Far3Det performance,
and demonstrate that validation and real-world performance can be significantly
improved by simply increasing the range of the training and validation datasets.
Code, models, and dataset are available at
https://github.com/robotaut/highway-scenes.

general and in surgical training in particular. Surgical training simulators
require fast and accurate deformable registration methods to provide a
realistic and instructive force feedback to the trainees. Towards this end, we
present a new evaluation study of different registration algorithms and
configurations and present our initial experience with the creation of a
benchmark dataset from CT and MRI of a canine foot. In addition, we present a
new metric, based on time warping, for quantifying the temporal alignment of
registration. Since the use of canine models in medical education is becoming
increasingly popular and there is currently no available publicly available
benchmark dataset for soft tissue available, we include a discussion on how to
create such a dataset from both MRI and CT modalities.
  We use a novel time warping distance metric to evaluate the alignment of the
registered deformations in time and space. In addition, we include a number of
common organs extracted from the MRI for improved evaluation. The evaluation is
performed using a variety of registration algorithms, including the FEM-based
Avocado library, the Finite Element Method solvers from COMSOL, NIfTI's
SyN, and Viscous Diffeomorphisms. We present a number of observations
demonstrating that SyN and Viscous Diffeomorphisms perform significantly
superior compared to the FEM-based methods, likely due to the relatively
coarse discretization and relatively large step sizes used in this study. We
also observe that SyN and Viscous Diffeomorphisms have a number of similarities
in their common vertices step. In addition, we observe that SyN performs
slightly better than the viscous diffeomorphisms when a number of organs are
included in the evaluation. Finally, we highlight the importance of careful
validation of registration algorithms for soft tissue using both MRI and CT
modalities.

learning system call filtering policies for containerized microservices
applications. At run-time, Timeloops automatically learns which system calls a
program should be allowed to invoke while rejecting attempts to call spurious
system calls. Further, Timeloops addresses many of the shortcomings of
state-of-the-art static analysis-based techniques, such as the ability to
generate tight filters for programs written in interpreted languages such as
PHP and Python, the ability to account for dynamic behavior such as memory
allocation and deallocation and network connections, and the ability to
incorporate application-specific semantic knowledge about the program to be
filtered. Timeloops consists of two components: a program analysis phase and a
filtering phase. The analysis phase uses a lightweight whole-program
instrumentation-based dynamic analysis to produce a call graph of the program
along with a set of the program's data structures. Then, using this call graph

  From astronomical point of view, the solar time is daily local time which
follow the daily movement of the Sun. In fact, it is not an absolute time but
relative time which dependent on latitude and daily position of the Sun. As
such, the solar time becomes repeated daily. In order to calculate the solar
time, Al-Khwarizmi in his book Al-Kitab al-Mawazena wa'l-Amwal gives several
formulas which are functions of latitude and declination of the Sun. Later on,
Al-Biruni in his book Al-Qanun al-Mas'udl gives more detailed calculation of
solar time which also take into account the equation of time. In turn, Ibn-Yunus
in his book Al-Zij al-Kabir gives more accurate calculation of solar time
which also take into account the latitude of the observer and the longitude of
the Sun. He also give table of solar time which cover one year.

clearly the development of Islamic astronomy in classical Islamic civilization.

of several Muslim astronomers. Later on, with the invention of mechanical
clock, the solar time becomes less important. However, with the modern trend of
preserving the classical knowledge of Islamic astronomy, the study of solar
time becomes highly demanded.

solitary wave solutions to the $\mathbf{U}(1)$-invariant Klein--Gordon equation
in one spatial dimension coupled to an anharmonic oscillator. We also give the
complete analysis of the spectrum of the linearization at a solitary wave.
Finally, we discuss the relation of this model to a one-dimensional
\emph{double} Klein--Gordon equation.
  Solitary wave solutions to the Klein--Gordon equation coupled to an harmonic
oscillator have been completely analyzed in a previous work. The anharmonic
oscillator case introduces a potential term in the oscillator equation that
changes the spectral properties of the problem. In this work we delimit the
range of values of the anharmonic coefficient for which solitary wave solutions
exist and we study their explicit properties.
  The potential anharmonic coefficient also affects the structure of the
spectral and orbital stability analysis. In particular, the use of conserved
quantities as tools to establish stability or instability in the anharmonic
case is different from the case of an harmonic oscillator. We discuss how to
use these quantities to establish stability or instability of solitary waves in
the anharmonic case.
  The study of the spectrum of the linearization at a solitary wave gives
information on the qualitative behavior of the solution of the Klein--Gordon
equation coupled to an anharmonic oscillator near the solitary wave. If the
spectrum does not contain positive eigenvalues then the solitary wave is
spectrally stable. If it contains at least one positive eigenvalue then it is
spectrally unstable. If all eigenvalues are nonpositive but the long-time
behavior of the solution is not explicitly known, then the orbital stability
of the solitary wave cannot be concluded.
  In the harmonic oscillator case, the spectrum of the linearization at a
solitary wave displayed several discrete eigenvalues, both positive and
nonpositive, and it was clear that the oscillating behavior of the harmonic
oscillator kept the solution bounded against the solitary wave. The presence of
these discrete eigenvalues also indicates that, in the anharmonic case, the
interplay between the oscillator and the Klein--Gordon equations must be such
that the solutions do not display the same richness of dynamics. In particular,
we observe that, differently from the harmonic case, the solitary wave solutions
are explicitly dependent on the anharmonic coefficient $\delta$.

(DE) in which the ultimate fate of the cosmos is a Big Rip, or alternatively
all the matter will be cycled through successive periods of expansion and
contraction in cyclic models [1-3]. In fact, the cyclic model is more
physically appealing because it does not need the introduction of a new form of
matter in the early universe. According to the cyclic paradigm, there was no
Big Bang in the classical sense, and our universe has always existed in some
form. The most well-known solution of this type is the model proposed by
Einstein-Cartan [4,5]. In this context, it is interesting to note that there
are proposals to relate the DE density with the graininess of space [6,7]. On
the other hand, there are several proposals for an IR cutoff [8,9]. In this
paper, we will investigate two HDE models with the Hubble radius [10] and the
graininess density as the IR cutoff [6,7], in an cyclic universe which evolves
without the Big Rip singularity. In addition, we will also consider two
universes: interacting and non-interacting.

systems displaying a nonequilibrium phase behavior. Here, we introduce
self-propulsion into a model of active Brownian particles with quenched disorder
and study its effect on the phase behavior of the active fluids formed from these
particles. Such ABPs with quenched disorder can be mapped to orientationally
ordered polar active Brownian particles with quenched disorder by an algebraic
change of variables and thus can show nematic fluctuations and a shear
stress-free nematic phase. Moreover, the self-propulsion can drive a chiral
phase in which the particles move collectively in a helical motion. We
numerically study the phase diagram of a suspension of such ABWs in two and
three dimensions. We find that in both dimensions the self-propulsion enhances
the strength of the nematic fluctuations and moves the nematic-to-isotropic
transition point towards lower concentrations of active particles. In three
dimensions, we also find that a purely chiral phase can be stabilized in a
sample with quenched parity breaking disorder at low concentrations of activity.
In two dimensions, the chiral phase is stabilized only in the presence of a
weak shear rate. We also find that the self-propulsion weakly affects the
orientational ordering in the isotropic phase but strongly affects the
magnetic and rotational symmetries of the nematic phase.
