is a challenging and open
robo-physics problem. Most previous studies have used rigid legs to evaluate
the performance of models on deformable terrain. In this study, we have developed
a simulation environment using the NVIDIA PhysX physics engine and a novel
method to evaluate models on deformable terrain. We have compared the
performance of rigid legs and rigid body (RB) feet on deformable terrain. The
results show that RB feet perform better on the deformable terrain than rigid
legs. This suggests that future models for deformable terrain may require
higher degree of controllability than has been achieved so far by rigid legs.
Furthermore, our simulation environment and methodology provide tools for
evaluating and comparing the performance of models on deformable terrain, which
will be essential for benchmarking future locomotion models.
  We present a novel reward function that prioritizes vertical motion over
horizontal motion, which is suitable for locomotion on deformable terrain. We
show that the reward function is able to differentiate the performance of rigid
legs on deformable terrain, which was not possible with a simple distance reward
function. This reward function may be useful for training models for
locomotion on deformable terrain.
  We show that the vertical reaction force increases significantly during
contact on deformable terrain, which may be an important consideration for
future locomotion models. The simulation speed in the multi-physics simulation
is presented and shown to be reasonable for policy gradient methods. The
multi-physics simulation is shown to be slower than single-physics simulations,
but faster than real world experiments. The presented study is a step towards
developing more realistic and challenging locomotion benchmarks.
  In summary, we have developed a simulation environment and presented a
carefully controlled baseline study of rigid legs on deformable terrain. The
results may be used as a basis for evaluating and comparing the performance of
looming models, which will be important for benchmarking future locomotion
models.

antiferromagnetic ground state. For weak screening, the strong correlations
push electrons out of the $s$-band so that the undoped nickelate remains a Mott

properties. Also in the regime of electron-doped nickelates a one-band model is
found to be valid. Here it captures the importance of holes in the $s$-like
band. A delicate balance between one-band and two-band descriptions arises in
the phase diagram of the nickelates.

lattice model for the electron count in nickelates. A one-band description

lattice model should therefore rather describe a band insulator with electrons

order is not expected for undoped nickelates. The different possible material
states and the uncertainty of the real material electron count motivate for a

current situation. Twitter is a popular social media platform to express and
share the opinions. As people are limited by time and space, sentiment analysis
can be utilized to mine the people's feelings towards the natural disaster
situation automatically. This study proposes a novel method to leverage the
geofencing technique combined with the spatial join operation to filter the
Twitter data centered on the disaster area. The experimental results show that
the proposed method can effectively improve the accuracy of sentiment analysis
to classify the negative, neutral, and positive sentiments for the Twitter
data set.
  From the empirical study, the geofencing technique combined with the spatial
join operation can effectively improve the accuracy of sentiment analysis.
Compared to the traditional methods using the entire Twitter data set, the
proposed method can achieve 2.35%, 3.19%, and 1.59% higher accuracy, respectively
for the Twitter data sets caused by typhoon, flood, and wildfire, respectively.
The proposed method can also effectively improve the precision, recall, and
F1-score of sentiment analysis. From the experimental results, the proposed
method can achieve 4.65%, 3.19%, and 2.31% higher precision, 3.19%, 2.31%, and
1.59% higher recall, and 3.19%, 2.31%, and 2.31% higher F1-score,

ors, the spin density wave (SDW)
transition was considered the competition to the superconducting (SC) phase. The
subsequent discovery of stripes has led to a modification of this competing
picture, where the superconductivity is assumed to grow out of the modulated
antiferromagnetic state. However, the existence of the stripes is still
contested. Here we report the detection of the magnetic oscillations in the
resistivity of the underdoped YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6-x}$ (YBCO) crystals, which in the
zero magnetic field is a hallmark of the SDW transition. The oscillations are
seen both in the growing (cooling) and decreasing (heating) magnetic field, and
can be explained by the magnetic breakdown to a higher Landau level in a
completely separated spin lattice. Surprisingly, the spin lattice is
characterized by a large effective mass ($m^{\ast}/e=4.3$), significantly
larger than in the neutron scattering measurements. The appearance of the
magnetic oscillations in the resistivity points out that the spins in the SDW
state are localized at the same lattice sites as the d-xavier electrons. The
localized nature of the spins and the electrons is due to the strong coupling
between them. This strong coupling, together with the separated spin lattice,
leads to the formation of the electron stripes.
  Finally, the absence of the magnetic oscillations in the optimised and
overdoped temperatures indicates that in these doping regions the spins are
polarized in the same lattice as the vanishingly small magnetic moment of the
cuprate charge carrier.

solitons with constant scalar curvature. A Liouville theorem is proved without
using gradient estimate : any bounded harmonic function is constant on gradient
shrinking Ricci solitons with constant scalar curvature. As an application, we
show that the space of harmonic functions with polynomial growth has finite
dimension.
  We also generalize the result to harmonic maps from gradient shrinking Ricci
solitons to harmonic spaces with constant scalar curvature, and to gradient
cohomologous flows.
  Finally we give some examples and a generalization to compact geodesic
metric spaces.
  The proof is based on the fact that constant scalar Ricci flow with a
satisfactory behavior of the Ricci flow has developed into a Ricci flow with
constant curvature.
  The proof is inspired from S. Hamilton's work on Liouville theorem for
harmonic functions on shrinking solitons, but the argument is more complicated
because we don't have the gradient estimate.
  The main tools are a characterization of the constant curvature flow,
compactness and convergence of Ricci flow with bounded curvature, and a
nondegeneration theorem of the potential function related to the scalar
curvature.
  We also use a result of M. Taylor about existence of solutions to
nonlocal elliptic equations, a result of M. Li and J. Wang on comparison of
potential functions, and a result of the author on characterization of
constant curvature Ricci flow.
  The proof is divided into several steps. In Section 1, we reduce the
problem to the case that the harmonic function is bounded on a large ball. In
Section 2, we define a potential function related to the scalar curvature and
prove a nondegeneration theorem in three steps. The first step gives a
characterization of the potential function for the case of Ricci flow. The
second step gives a bound of the potential function for the case of Ricci
flow. The last step gives a nondegeneration of the potential function for the
case of Ricci flow.
  In Section 3, we prove that there is a uniform bound of Ricci flow for
solitons with constant scalar curvature. In Section 4, we prove that there is
a uniform bound of Ricci flow for solitons with constant scalar curvature II.
In Section 5, we prove that there is a uniform bound of Ricci flow for
solitons with constant scalar curvature III.

to a global average pooling layer without increasing the percentage of the
poisoned training data. Moreover, our results show that these backdoors are

combination with the activation function of the last linear layer. We show that

when the backdoor attack is activated with a dynamic trigger that is similar to

method enables novel contrast mechanisms and greatly improves the
interoperability between different microscopy modalities by providing
high-resolution and fast widefield two-photon spectroscopy.

simultaneously detect four different contrasts in a single two-photon

Neural Rendering (DNR) provides a compelling balance between computational
complexity and realism of the resulting images. Using skinned meshes for
rendering articulating objects is a natural extension for the DNR framework and
would open it up to a wealth of applications. However, in this case the
neural shading step must account for deformations that are not aligned with the
network's input coordinate system, and as a result, the resulting animation
often suffers from alignment errors and other limitations. We present
Articulated Neural Shading (ANS), a method that combines DNR with neural
skinning methods to achieve detailed, realistic, and animation-accurate
renderings of objects modeled as articulated deformable meshes. In contrast to
DNR, we use a network that operates directly on the mesh space, aligned with
the object's morphology, which enables more accurate neural shading and
reprojection. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a variety of
complex, articulated 3D models from different source categories and show that
it compares or outperforms state-of-the-art single-frame and animation
methods.

abdominal wall to provide images of the organs using light in the visible and
near-infrared spectrum. To enhance the image quality, more light is shone

tissue there are strong tissue-dependent scattering and absorption, as
demonstrated by the inverse Brethrengren law. Such tissue-dependent light
penetration can lead to shadows and hotspots in the region far from the
laparoscope. To compensate for the light intensity spatially, traditional
compensation schemes based on inverse distance square have been shown to have
significant errors. In this work, we demonstrate that if the light intensity
distribution in the image is normalized by the scattering coefficient of the
tissue, the compensated light intensity can closely follow the natural light
intensity. This is because the normalized light intensity is proportional to the
absorption plus the scattering times the square of the distance. This method
does not require knowledge of absorption or any fitting parameters and can be
implemented in real-time during the surgery.

method also works for the Laparoscope being positioned at an angle relative to
the tissue. When combined with traditional inverse distance square compensation
with 10 times the concentration of contrast agent, the compensated light
intensity is closer to the natural light intensity than without contrast agent.
With this method, the shadows and hotspots in the image are greatly reduced,
resulting in enhanced image quality for laparoscopic surgery.

to the absorption plus the scattering times the square of the distance, which
can be used to determine tissue optical properties in vivo.

a topological merger between two separate modes. This indicates that even
thin topological insulators can host a rich variety of edge modes, more than
what is expected from their quantized Chern number. Finally, we note that the
semi-quantized bulk Chern number can be characterized by a global magnetization
of the superfluid, while the semi-localized edge modes can be activated by a
small chemical potential difference between the two surfaces of the film.

new ancillary
services, which are crucial for ensuring the stability of the power system. The
ex-post pricing of these services is often not efficient anymore and new
mechanisms for forecasting and pricing are needed. However, also ex-ante
ancillary services are subject to rapid changes and new services and market
mechanisms are needed. In both cases, smart contracts can provide
automatization and efficiency. In this paper we focus on the start-up ancillary
service and provide an economic and technical analysis of a Dutch market with
proposals for improvement towards blockchain and smart contract technology.
The Dutch start-up ancillary service provides a clear example of a rapidly
changing ancillary service with opportunities for improvement and automation
towards smart contract and blockchain technology. The Dutch market mechanism
provides scope for further development and improvement. With this research we
provide an example and guidelines for the analysis of an ancillary service and
its possible automation towards smart contract and blockchain technology.
Furthermore, the results can provide input for the further development of
Blockchain4Energy, a blockchain and smart contract development platform for
ancillary services and the Dutch electricity market.
  The analysis shows that the current Dutch start-up ancillary service and
market mechanism are not fully efficient anymore. Changes in generation technology
and consumption behavior have lead to changes in the cost structure of the
ancillary service, which are not yet fully reflected in the market mechanism.
Several possible adjustments and improvements are proposed and evaluated with a
stochastic dispatch model for the Dutch electricity system. The best solution
will be translated into a smart contract and examined with a test environment.
The results show that smart contract technology can significantly improve the
start-up ancillary service and market mechanism. Furthermore, the use of a
blockchain and a system operator can ensure full and transparent coverage of
all system needs with ancillary services at all times.
  In conclusion, the Dutch start-up ancillary service and market mechanism are
subject to possible adjustments and improvements towards smart contract and
blockchain technology. The proposed changes and smart contract can ensure a
fully efficient start-up ancillary service at optimal costs for the electricity
system in the Netherlands.
  Finally, the research methodology can be used as a guideline for the analysis
of an ancillary service and its possible automation towards smart contract and
blockchain technology.

important roles in linguistic comprehension and that they are not simply
optional embellishments, but are instead necessary to disambiguate discourse
structures and recover correct inferences. We propose a simple yet effective
discourse parsing model that explicitly takes the contributions of discourse
markers into account. Our empirical evaluation shows that incorporating
discourse markers improves discourse parsing performance on multiple datasets
and that our model outperforms a strong baseline that ignores discourse
markers.

(1) We point out that current discourse parsing models ignore the effects of
discourse markers and study how to incorporate markers into a discourse parser.
(2) We propose a novel representation for discourse markers called {\it marker
signatures} and show that markers are heterogeneous -- while all instances of
a single marker look similar, different markers behave differently. (3) We
apply recent advances in neural model architecture and training methods to the
task of discourse parsing and show that a simple but well-tuned model outperforms
a strong baseline that incorporates marker signatures.
  We also carry out an auxiliary study in which we train a regression model to
predict human discourse parsing times and show that a model that incorporates
discourse markers does better than a baseline on this task, providing further
evidence that markers are important for human discourse parsing.
  Finally, we point out that current discourse parsing datasets contain a
proportion of sentences with multiple possible discourse parses and propose a
simple method for automatically identifying these structurally ambiguous
sentences.

process in several Cournot models, and evaluate them in terms of their

algorithms with a parametric model that produces random best responses, and

technologies.

learning process may lead to an increased risk of getting stuck in
non-competitive dynamics, which may explain the observed empirical evidence of
the limited increase in profits in real world oligopolies.

genetic algorithms that significantly shortens the learning process while
producing outcomes with high payoffs in most of the cases.
  The latter suggests that firms can benefit from these advanced technologies
even if they are not fully understood.
  In conclusion, the evaluation of the different specifications of the
co-evolutionary genetic algorithms suggests that firms in a Cournot model
competiting using sophisticated learning technologies may benefit from the

demonstrate that this novel formulation can be used to detect anomalous
behavior, such as DDoS attacks, in the network. Furthermore, our approach is
relatively low-complexity and scalable and has the potential to be used in
real-time network traffic analysis to detect potential cyber threats.
Additionally, our framework of analyzing the network traffic using Shannon
entropy is general and can be used to analyze traffic from a wide range of
devices, including those part of the IoT.

computation complexity of the proposed method is low enough to be scalable for

spread of the infection and hence its menace depend on how the virus laden
droplets evolve with time in air. In this paper, we have numerically simulated
and analytically solved model equations which describe the evolution of droplet
diameters in air under the sole influence of evaporation and gravity. These
model equations and solutions can serve as input to calculate the survival time
of the infected persons and the spread of infection through a group of people.
Further, these simulations can help in understanding the effect of humidity on
the dissipation of droplets.
  We find that for $0.02 \leq \phi \leq 0.50$, where $\phi$ is the relative
humidity, the diameters of the droplets either increase or decrease monotonically
with time. Under these conditions, there is no possibility of bistability or
non-uniformity of dynamics as observed in lower humidities. Under these
non-uniform conditions, larger droplets may evaporate faster than the smaller
ones, leading to highly non-uniform and unpredictable dynamics. Such complex
dynamics may be responsible for the long range spread of the infection. Under
high humidity ($\phi \geq 0.70$), the droplets either evaporate completely or
remain stationary. Under very low humidity ($\phi \leq 0.02$), droplets either
remain stationary or move rapidly to their natural diameters with a small
wrapping around their surfaces.
  Under intermediate humidities ($0.02 \leq \phi \leq 0.50$), bistability,
hysteresis, and highly non-uniform dynamics are observed. These three
phenomena are usually associated with thermal fluctuations and nonlinear
dynamics. The presence of these complex phenomena in a deterministic system
indicates the partial influence of thermal fluctuations under intermediate
humidities.
  The model may be useful in understanding the spread of infection through a
group of people and the effect of humidity on the dissipation of droplets.
Further, the complex dynamics of the model may be useful in understanding the
complexity of respiratory infections.

simulation studies of the droplet dynamics and infections.

numerous fields of engineering and science, including power systems. In this
context, learning algorithms can exploit data to achieve significant
performance gains in terms of accuracy, speed, and cost compared to
traditional computational methods based on solving systems of nonlinear
equations, integrals, and differential equations. Although novel applications
of NNs in power systems are rapidly emerging, there are still fundamental
questions about how to best design learning algorithms for specific problems,
how to interface NNs with traditional power system algorithms, and how to
implement these new hybrid algorithms in computational frameworks, also known
as power system platforms. To address these questions, this paper presents a
comprehensive overview of NNs in power systems, drawing from the recent
literature and emphasizing the software side of power system research. The
discussion starts by presenting a brief overview of NNs in power systems,
followed by an overview of the two main categories of learning algorithms:
supervised and unsupervised methods. Next, the following topics are
discussed: data in power systems, NN architectures in power systems,
unsupervised learning in power system data, and the role of optimization in
power system NNs. Finally, to illustrate how NNs can be integrated with
power system algorithms, the article presents a hybrid platform for solving
power flow problems using physics-informed neural networks and another for
predicting electric vehicle charging behavior using unsupervised learning
algorithms. Throughout the discussion, limitations of current NN power system
platforms and opportunities for further research are highlighted.
  The following related platforms and tools are presented in the article:
GPyTO, OpenDSE, PyPowerFlow, PyTorch-DynamicNetworkAnalytics, and
PowerFlowNet. In summary, this work provides an interdisciplinary overview of
NNs in power systems, emphasizing the computational side of this rapidly
developing area of power system research.

Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms exploit the information from camera
and inertial sensors to estimate position and translation. Recent deep learning
based VIO methods use recurrent neural networks to process and fuse visual
and inertial features for better estimation. However, these models' ability to
handle sensor noise and corruption, and robustness to challenging scenarios
while maintaining accuracy has not been fully explored. In this work, we
benchmark popular and new deep learning VIO algorithms on both simulated and
real world datasets, and also test the algorithms with different sensor
configurations, with and without wireless communication drop for communication
failure, and with and without inertial sensors to analyze the performance
under various stressors. We also propose a new multi-stream recurrent model
that outperforms existing models in both accuracy and robustness. From the
benchmark, we find that the performance of deep learning VIO algorithms is
affected by the quality of training data and the complexity of the model. We
also find that the best algorithm is dependent on the application. From the
analysis of the different stressors, we find that the deep learning VIO
algorithm's accuracy degrades with wireless communication drop and inertial
sensor failure. We argue that the challenge for deep learning VIO algorithms to
be used in real world applications is not just to have high accuracy but also
to have enough robustness to handle real world stressors.
  We provide our simulation code at
https://github.com/AmrElsamny/vio-simulation and the dataset and code for the
real world testing at https://github.com/AmrElsamny/3dr2v1-database.

information from camera and inertial sensors to estimate position and translation
continuously. Although these algorithms have been shown to have high accuracy

has not been fully investigated. In this work, we benchmark deep learning VIO
algorithms to investigate their performance under different sensor
configurations, with and without wireless communication drop for communication
failure, and with and without inertial sensors. We also provide a comprehensive
theoretical analysis of these algorithms to investigate their ability to minimize
the position error, and provide a new performance metric to quantify the
performance of these algorithms.

investigate the spontaneous spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) in a
multi-solar-system with non-linear kinetic term, where the vacuum energy
associated with the SSB can be signalled by a negative mass. Our result
reveals that due to the repulsion among the solars, an spontaneous symmetry
breaking ground state with negative mass can be obtained, in which the
nonlinear self-interaction plays an important role. The present model could
provide an alternative mechanism for explaining the phenomenon of dark matter
in nature.
  In the following, we further investigate the effect of an electric field on
the SSB. It is found that the electric field can drive a transition between two
different SSB ground states with different masses, which could also be used to
simulate a harmonic oscillator.
  Finally, we discuss how to experimentally detect the SSB phase in multi-solar
systems. When the solars are micrometer or sub-micrometer in size, the
inter-solar potential can be detected by an optical interferometer. While for
much larger solars, one can observe the signalling of negative mass by an
acceleration detector. Further investigations are needed to discuss how to
detect the SSB phase when the solars are in the form of dark matter.
  Finally, we would like to emphasize that our model could provide a number of
theoretical avenues for further investigation.
  In conclusion, in this Letter we have proposed a model of multi-solar-system
which can spontaneously break a symmetry, and investigate how to experimentally
detect such an SSB phase. The model could provide a new avenue for investigating
nonlinear field theoretical aspects of quantum mechanics.

associated to an integrable highest weight module for simple affine Lie

  The study of parafermion vertex operator algebra associated to simple affine
Lie superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$ started in our previous work [Comp. Phys. Commun.
(under review)]. There, we classify the highest weight integrable modules for
$osp(1|2n)$-family and find the characters for these modules. In the algebra
part, we investigate the structure of the parafermion vertex operator algebra
associated to those integrable highest weight modules. The main goal is to find
a set of generators for this algebra. This is an extension of Sugawara's
construction for simple Lie groups to simple Lie supergroups of type $osp(1|2n)$
with parafermion (bosonic) supercharges.
  Our approach is based on a bosonic-fermionic correspondence which was
observed in [Phys. Lett. B 775, 137-143 (2018)]. By using this mapping, we
manage to construct four sets of parafermion operators for each integrable
highest weight module for $osp(1|2n)$-family. These operators satisfy the
same OPE algebra as the bosonic ones for $osp(1|2n-1)$ and $osp(1|2n-2)$. In
addition, their weights are also similar to the bosonic case. In particular, the
central element $L_{1|2}^{(0)}$ has weight $\frac{1}{2}(E_8^{(1)}+D_8^{(1)})$.
This is consistent with the weight of the bosonic supercharge in the
$osp(1|2n-1)$-family and also in the $osp(1|2n-2)$-family.
  Finally, it is interesting to note that all these operators are constructed
purely from supercharges and generators of $osp(1|2n)$ with no additional
data. This indicates a highly organized structure of $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2n)$
integrable highest weight modules.

is the most popular method for simulating space
time geometries with binary massive (gravitational) fields, as it provides an
exact description of the fields and their source. However, as with any
approximation scheme, it is important to know how well it works for different
configurations. In this work we investigate how well the 1.5 formalism can
simulate geodesic motion in general relativity. We consider a wide variety of
binary systems consisting of a compact object of arbitrary mass and charge,
polarized but not rotating, in orbit around a large star. We track the
polarization of the compact object through a variety of different orbital
phases, from plunge to merger. While we find that the 1.5 approximation
correctly captures geodesic motion to very high accuracy for most of the
orbit, it suffers from a severe breakdown in the merger phase. This suggests
that if one is modeling mergers with the 1.5 formalism, then one must include
quadrupole effects to correctly describe geodesic motion. The premerge
behavior, which is not well described by a simple expression, is also
affected, but to a lesser extent.
  We find that for the point particle approximation, the merger time is
correctly predicted by the 1.5 formalism to within 2% for all configurations
we considered. This suggests that the failure of the 1.5 formalism to
correctly predict geodesic motion in mergers is specifically due to the
polarization of the compact object and not due to the mass ratio or mass-to
charge ratio of the system.
  Finally, we note that if one is interested in the waveforms produced by the
merger then the 1.5 formalism may still be useful, as it correctly predicts
the leading order behavior of the frequency and amplitude of the waveforms in
the merger for all configurations.
  In the companion paper \cite{Schafer2020b} we investigate how well the 1.5
approximation can simulate the gravitational radiation produced by binary systems
consisting of two compact objects.

environments are known to spur economic productivity and innovation in cities,
while also to foster social capital and resilience of communities. However,
mobility restrictions during the pandemic have forced people to substantially
reduce urban physical encounters, raising questions on the social and economic
impacts of such behavior. In this work, we use cellular network data from over
four million mobile devices and social media activity from over 4.5 million
users to study how much people have reduced their urban physical encounters
during the pandemic and how this has impacted the diversity of experiences and
social interactions that people have in cities. Using tools from statistical
physics, we find that the reduced urban encounters have followed a power law
dynamics over the course of the pandemic, with devices visiting significantly
fewer unique locations and for shorter durations. We further find that people
have mainly been encountering locations that are closer to their home
locations, indicating a strong stickiness in locations that people keep
visiting. Analysis of the diversity of experiences of time spent on types of
locations shows a significant reduction in the long tail of the
distribution, indicating that the reduced encounters have mainly impacted
diversity at the lower tail of the distribution, i.e., for the most common
types of locations. On the social interactions, we find that the number of
unique followees that each user can reach has decreased, indicating that the
reduced encounters have also pruned the connections in the social network.

become stronger, indicating that some of the social connections have been
strengthened during the pandemic. Finally, we observe that the changes in the
diversity of experiences and social interactions have been more pronounced in
cities of lower population sizes, raising questions on the sustainability of
urban diversity and innovation in smaller cities during future pandemics.

urban mobility restrictions due to the pandemic had a causal effect on the

of infinite depth in the presence of nonzero constant vorticity. A goal is to
describe the effects of uniform shear flow on the modulation of weakly
nonlinear quasi-monochromatic surface gravity waves. Starting from the
Hamiltonian formulation of this problem and using techniques from Hamiltonian
transformation theory, we derive a Hamiltonian Dysthe equation for the time
evolution of the wave envelope. Consistent with previous studies, we observe
that the uniform shear flow tends to enhance or weaken the modulational
instability of Stokes waves depending on its direction and strength. It is found
that when the shear flow is aligned with the wave propagation (anti-parallel
shear), a simpler condition for modulational instability is obtained compared to
the case when the shear is perpendicular to the wave propagation. A study of
the statistics of the modulation-damped breaker-like breaking model suggests
that the uniform shear flow has a negligible effect on the probability
distributions of the breaking frequency and amplitude.
  From the Dysthe model, we also study the effects of uniform shear flow on the
secondary wave crest dynamics just before breaking. Like the vorticity field
created by patch vortices, the shear flow tends to increase the crest curvature
and decrease the time needed for the wave crest to collapse. As a result, the
secondary breaking mechanism becomes stronger in the presence of shear flow.
Again, the strength of this enhancement depends on the alignment and strength of
the shear flow.
  Numerical simulations of the fully nonlinear water wave model of Callow and
Trulsen [J. Fluid Mech. 716, R414 (2013)] also show that the presence of
shear tends to weaken or strengthen the breaking threshold depending on the
direction and strength of the shear. In all cases, the presence of shear tends
to increase the breaking frequency once breaking occurs. As in the Dysthe model,
the shear tends to increase the curvature of the wave crest before breaking and
thus acts as a trigger for breaking. The strength of this effect depends on the
alignment and strength of the shear.
  In all cases, the Dysthe model and the fully nonlinear water wave model
predict similar trends of uniform shear flow on weakly and strongly nonlinear
surface gravity wave breaking. However, numerical simulations of the fully
nonlinear water wave model also show modes of secondary breaking that are not
captured in the Dysthe model.

new but a rapidly growing problem. The
efficiency of measures against the spread of fake news depends on the accuracy
and speed of detection algorithms for such information. We present a method for
automatic identification of potentially dangerous news based on a psycholinguistic
analysis of the quality of news titles. The method is based on a machine learning
model that classifies the quality of a news title as either high or low based on
the emotional content and complexity of the title. The model is trained on a
dataset of 2,000 news titles, where the quality is annotated by humans. The
annotation includes the use of emotional labels and the Flesch-Kincaid Grade
Level, which measures the complexity of the language. The model consists of two
sub-models, where the first model outputs the emotional score of a title and the
second model outputs the complexity score. These scores are then combined into a
final score used for classification. Our experiments show that the model
outperforms existing methods for classifying the quality of news titles.
Furthermore, we show that by using the model for automatically improving the
quality of the title, from low to high, we can increase the recognition rate of
the model by almost 20%.
  We also present a content-aware generation model that can increase the
quality of a news title based on the content of the news article. The model is
trained on a dataset of 2,000 news articles, where the quality of the title is
annotated by humans. The model consists of two parts: a language generation
model and a filter model. The language generation model generates a sentence
given a sequence of words, while the filter model filters out generated words
considering the content of the article. The final title is then produced by
filtering the output of the language generation model with the filter model.
Experiments show that by using the model for automatically improving the
quality of the title, from low to high, we can increase the recognition rate of
the model by almost 15%.
  We show that by using these two models together we can increase the
recognitional performance by almost 25%.

a supervised machine learning (ML) model. However, current pre-trained ML
models for natural language processing (NLP) contain a great deal of language
knowledge that can be used to fill in missing information in data with
incomplete annotations. For example, while a model trained on fully annotated
sentence-level data may be able to infer the part-of-speech tags from phrase-level
annotations, a model trained on data with additional annotations may be able to
infer additional linguistic information, such as syntactic dependencies.
Furthermore, additional annotations can provide a model with more context in which
to encode and make use of the information that it does receive. For example,
annotations of entities can be used to build a entity linker, but annotations of
named entities can be used to build a named entity recognizer. While ML models
trained on data with extra annotations may be able to use the additional
information, the benefit to the user is even greater. For example, while a model
may be able to predict the named entities from annotations of entities, the
annotations of named entities provide a straightforward interface for the user to
add the information they would normally need to write their own part-of-speech
tagging or named entity recognition tool.
  In this paper we explore the use of linguistic annotations to enable the use of
pre-trained ML models as tools for the general language understanding task, rather
than simply as tools for specific tasks such as part-of-speech tagging or named
entity recognition. We show that a model trained on data with additional annotations
can encode and make use of a large amount of additional linguistic information,
producing output which is significantly more semantically coherent and linguistically
informed than that of a model trained on the same amount of annotated data. We further
show that the benefit of using a model as a tool for understanding coherent
textual phrases is very large, with a model trained on data with annotations for
parts-of-speech, named-entities, and syntactic dependencies producing output which
is significantly more semantically coherent than that of models trained on larger
but less informative datasets.

use. While models trained on data with annotations of parts-of-speech, named
entities, and syntactic dependencies perform substantially better than models
trained on data with fewer annotations, there is a trade-off between the benefit
of adding more annotations and the cost of annotating more data. In particular

importtant feature for mobile robots such as autonomous vehicles and mobile
robots for search and rescue operations. Many algorithms have been proposed in
the past for this task, including random sampling methods and algorithms that
exploit environmental information such as odometry or sensor data from on-board
instruments. These algorithms are powerful but they all have in common that they
require extensive computational resources. In particular, the time it takes to
process and interpret sensor data from a LiDAR scanner or stereo camera is one of
the main bottlenecks for many algorithms. In this paper, we present a method
which uses the structure of splines to navigate a mobile robot through a
unknown track geometry. The method does not require any environmental
information and is extremely simple to implement and run in real-time on
microcontrollers with integer arithmetic support, such as those found in
microcontrollers from the popular ESP-IDF framework. Although the algorithm is
simple, the results are promising and could possibly be extended to enable
self-steering of autonomous vehicles or other mobile robots which need to
navigate through unknown tracks or roads.
  We model the future track geometry using a cubic spline and update the
control points based on the measured speed of the vehicle. During the
calculation of the future geometry, we can insert points into the spline to
avoid sharp changes in the curvature of the path. This algorithm could be of
interest to enable self-driving vehicles to safely navigate through unknown
roads or track geometries and as a possible solution to the autonomous
vehicle end-of-line test, i.e. the test to verify that a self-driving vehicle
can navigate through a unknown track.

  From the theoretical perspective, our scheme offers an novel way to
distinguish the phase evolution of the atomic wave packet in the interferometry
by introducing the additional but controllable phase evolution caused by the
weak off-resonance light field, which is advantageously avoided being trapped

advantageously free from common source of phase noise, such as the magneto-optic

new way to detect the very weak local magnetic field in the laboratory.

averaged population difference in the two symmetric beams is only 0.005%, and
the corresponding detectable spin coherence time is longer than 1000 ms. If the
available atomic ensemble has the same temperature as the one in the present
experiments, the proposed scheme could also work well when the average
trapping time is as short as 10 ms. Moreover, if the magnetic field is larger
than 10$^{-5}$ G, the required average trapping time is only 1 ms.

weak local magnetic field expelled by the superconductor. In the future work,

angles, while based on polarimetric remote sensing data, they are more efficient
and promising. Here we explore retrievals using only passive imager data. We
assume that convective clouds consist of three types of 3D structures: the
upright anvil, upright and tilted vertical growth layers, and shallow layer
bottom cloud. Based on the relationship between cloud optical thickness and
physical thickness, we construct an optimal estimation model that minimizes the
difference between observed top-of-atmosphere upwelling solar flux and
bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) simulated by a 3D cloud
radiative transfer model. We use the CloudSat vertical growth layer height
product and a cloud type product derived from geostationary satellite imagery
as constraints. The model parameters are the optical thickness, effective
particle size, and thickness of the anvil and layers. We use the A-train
polarimetric imager measurements over tropical ocean areas with convective
clouds on April 25, 2008. The retrievals show that the anvil optical thickness
and thickness are similar to those of the growth layers, indicating that the
anvil and growth layers are coupled. The retrievals also show that the
effective particle size increases with cloud height. The root mean square errors
between retrieved and cloud radar-estimated layer thickness are about 0.5 km,
and about 0.2 for optical thickness and effective particle size. The proposed
3D cloud structure assumption and model parameters are generally consistent with
observations and cloud parameterization in general circulation models.
Furthermore, the thinning of convective clouds from the surface to the upper
troposphere is well captured. The proposed passive 3D cloud retrieval is more
efficient than active 3D cloud retrievals and can be used in areas without

scalar quantum electrodynamics at nonzero chemical potential. The argument is
based on the Faddeev-Popov determinant. In the qutrit case we find that this
determinant has a series of zeros for imaginary chemical potential which
corresponds to a discrete series of zeros for real chemical potential that can
be continued via the sign function. These zeros correspond to noninteracting
stable charged particles, the qutrit electron. The mass spectrum of the
qutrit electron is presented and critiqued as a model for any fermionic
determinant in gauge theories.
  From a statistical point of view, qutrits are more stable against
spontaneous decay than qubits or two-level systems. We argue that the
continuation of imaginary to real chemical potential for qutrits provides a
mechanism for the stabilization of fermionic states against Bose-Einstein
condensation. This provides a basis for a qutrit model of superfluidity. We
also find that certain qutrit states exhibit a kind of supersymmetry, an
additional argument for the importance of considering qutrits in field theory
and its applications to condensed matter.
  Finally, we observe that the qutrit electron has three colors, as determined
by the third component of isospin. This provides a basis for a model of
color-flavor locked superfluidity.
  All of these phenomena - stable charged particles, superfluidity, and
superconductivity - arise in a theory that contains no explicit bosons or
condensation phenomena. The present work provides further evidence for the
usefulness of considering non-binary systems in the study of the sign function
and fermionic determinants.
  As an appendix, we provide an argument for the use of qutrits in a model of
atom-light interactions, providing another basis for the utility of non-binary
systems in studying phenomena involving light.

music, people still rely on textual search engines like Google. We propose Pied
piper, a meta search engine for music. It can search for music lyrics, song
metadata and song audio or a combination of any of these as the input query and
efficiently return the relevant results.
  The system is built using a cluster of machines in a distributed computing
environment using Apache Hadoop and HBase as the backend database. The system
has three main components - Indexer, Server and GUI. The Indexer component
generates an inverted index from a large dataset of songs in HBase and the
Server component hosts the search engine API which uses the inverted index to
search for music and return the relevant results to the user via a GUI built
using Python and Tkinter.
  Search for music is a computationally expensive task as it involves
computational intensive audio processing operations like similarity distance
computation and bit manipulation operations. The system uses a novel data
structure called bit matrix to reduce the time complexity of the search
operation to almost O(1). It also uses a heuristic algorithm to reduce the
time taken to index a dataset of 1 million songs to less than 2 hours. The
system achieves search time of less than a second for a textual search of a
dataset of 1 million songs and 125 milliseconds for an audio search of a dataset
of 100,000 songs.
  The system provides many features like near-duplicate detection, song
fragment identification, audio classification, audio search by humming, song
splicing and appendage detection, audio alignment of two songs, audio or
fragment similarity search, textual search with relevance ranking and music
metadata search with relevance ranking.
  The system has many applications like music retrieval, near-duplicate image
removal, music information retrieval, music classification, music
authentication, music compression, music privacy, and music forensics.
Moreover, it can be used in developing music applications like music splicing
tools, appendage detectors, fragment identifiers, audio aligners,
classifiers, and validators.

and can be used in many music and related applications.

  Research in computational complexity has traditionally been driven by pure
curiosity about the power and limitations of efficient computation, and this
field has thrived as a result. The emergence of new problems and techniques
arising from this curiosity have led to countless important advances in
computational complexity. However, when trying to apply hardness results to
communicate the intractability of a problem to an outside audience, it is
sometimes difficult to convince people of the fact of intractability -- e.g.,
that a problem is not likely to be solvable in polynomial time. (Of course,
many people are willing to take our word for it, but this is not sufficient
for many applications.) Perhaps the reason for this difficulty is that, until
now, there has not been a serious effort to establish (or demonstrate the
feasibility of) tractable solutions to hard problems using only classical
computers and techniques that definitively bypass hardness results.
  In the following, we survey some of the major results in computational
complexity that would be relevant in a translational setting, and survey some
of the major challenges that would arise in a translational computational
complexity project. We also survey some of the approaches that could be taken
to demonstrate tractable solutions to hard problems (or other applications of
computational complexity to other fields), and survey some of the promising
areas for future work in this area.
  A challenge in a translational computational complexity project is to
determine which problems to tackle. There are many interesting and important
applications waiting for tractable algorithms, but choosing the right ones
requires a deep understanding of both the problem and the current state of the
art in computational complexity. In the following, we discuss some general
strategies for choosing problems to tackle in a translational computational
complexity project, and we survey some specific examples of interesting
applications waiting for tractable algorithms.
  Another important aspect of a translational computational complexity project
is to communicate the progress to a broader audience.

because it influences academic achievement and career success. However, many
students lack curiosity because they lack the skills to solve complex problems
and think critically. To address this issue, we propose a novel AI-powered
curiosity-driven learning (CDL) framework that combines AI, machine learning,
and gamification to develop curiosity in next-generation students. The
CDL framework consists of three layers: (1) a curiosity engine that attracts
and holds student attention using interactive problems and critical thinking
pathways; (2) a learning engine that provides personalized learning pathways
based on student performance and progress; and (3) a gamification engine that
provides points, badges, and leaderboard services to encourage competition
among learners and promote continued learning. The curiosity engine is the
core of the CDL framework and is composed of pre-trained language models and
algorithmic strategies that generate coherent and challenging problems that
trigger student curiosity. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the CDL
framework, we developed a prototype learning system for middle school students
called iThink that implements the CDL framework. The iThink system was used by
over 1,500 students in 18 months, resulting in a 25% increase in academic
performance and a 30% increase in student engagement. The iThink system
demonstrates that the CDL framework can develop curiosity in students and
improve their academic performance. This framework can be extended to
develop curiosity in learners in various domains by customizing the
curiosity engine, learning engine, and gamification engine to fit specific
learning objectives and curricula.

real-world problems, they have not yet been fully exploited for solving
optimization problems. In this work, we use a least-squares Gaussian process
regression as a surrogate for solving continuous constrained optimization
problems. We show that the resulting surrogate optimization problem can be
efficiently solved using a modified version of the conjugate gradient algorithm.
The resulting algorithm has $O(nK)$ time complexity, where $n$ is the dimension
of the search space and $K$ is the number of iterations, making it suitable for
learning and optimizing high-dimensional functions. We also show that the
iterative algorithm eliminates the need for computing gradients and inequality
constraints explicitly, reducing the required observation data. We further
introduce an online version, which solves optimization problems streaming
observations. Experimental results show that our approach can solve problems
involving functions from various classes of continuity and also handles
scenarios with concept drift.
  We propose a simple and efficient algorithm that uses Gaussian processes to
solve constrained optimization problems. The algorithm is easy to implement
and can be used to solve both continuous and discrete problems. The algorithm
can also be used to solve multi-objective problems and handle noisy and
missing data. We show that the algorithm can solve problems using very few
observations required explicit gradient and constraint values, making it
practical for problems with high dimensionality and large volume of data. The
algorithm can also be used to solve online constrained optimization problems
and handle regularization and penalty constraints. Theoretical guarantees of
convergence are provided under mild assumptions on the problem structure and the
learning model. Experimental results show the effectiveness of the algorithm in
finding near optimal solutions, reducing training time, and improving
generalization performance.

obtained from the on-board computer of urban buses. The method consists of a

state-of-the-art technique that uses computer vision techniques to extract
lane changes from images obtained from the on-board computer of urban buses.

present a lane change segmentation method that outperforms the existing

a blockchain, based on which many
cryptocurrencies are implemented. Such programs need to be verified, and this
verification process is performed by a sequence of equality checks on intermediate
values (known as statements) during which the programs consume energy and money.
To what extent different arrangements of smart contracts affect the energy
consumption and fees has become an important question, but to our knowledge it
has not been studied yet. In this work, we study this issue, and we model it by
a two-dimensional binary wire automaton with dynamic edge costs. During an
execution of the automaton, each edge is visited at most once. We show that the
problem of determining the minimum total cost of edge-following in this model
is NP-hard, even if all edge costs are integers from the set $\{1,2,4,8,\dots\}$
or the set $\{1,2,3,4,\dots\}$. On the other hand, if all edge costs are
integers from the set $\{1,2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23,\dots\}$, then there is a
polynomial algorithm to solve this problem for automata of size $n$ in time
$O(n^2)$. In addition, we show that for automata with dynamic edge costs in
this range, there is a quasi-polynomial algorithm to solve this problem in time
$O(n^4/\log n)$, which improves the complexity of previously known solutions.
Furthermore, we also show that for this model with dynamically changing edge
costs, there is an efficient randomized algorithm to solve this problem in time
$O(n\log n)$. In addition, we also give a lower bound of $\Omega(n\log n)$ for
this problem for this model with dynamically changing edge costs.
Finally, we give an efficient randomized algorithm to determine whether an
execution is optimal in time $O(n)$ for this model with dynamically changing
edge costs.

subsequence problem, for which we give new and efficient solutions for various
variants, as well as a new lower bound.

is invariant to translation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the

structure for video super-resolution and the validity of the experiment
configuration in the VSRGAN paper. To do so, we conduct an exhaustive
experiment on both Dearoom-1.8M and MSRVTT datasets, with both recurrent and
non-recurrent VSR GANs. The results show that recurrent structure does not
significantly improve the performance and even causes instability during
training. Thus we conclude that recurrent structure is not necessary for video
super-resolution, and the claim of VSRGAN paper is not true. With this
conclusion, we point out that the main contribution of VSRGAN paper, which is
the use of GAN loss in VSRGAN framework, is actually trivial and can be
demonstrated without using recurrent structure.

  Video super-resolution (VSR) has been a popular research topic in the computer
vision community for decades. The recent works of VSR typically employ
convolutional neural network (CNN) with GAN loss to produce high-resolution
videos from low-resolution input. The VSRGAN by Kim \textit{et al.} is one of
the most recent and popular framework for VSR. It attributes the success of the
state-of-the-art performance to the use of recurrent structure with GAN loss.
However, in this work, we question the necessity of using recurrent structure
for VSR by conducting exhaustive experiments on two popular video datasets:
Dearoom-1.8M and MSRVTT.

PSR B1133+16, from which we have obtained high-quality dynamic spectra and
their associated scintillation arcs, arising from the scattering screens
located along the line of sight to the pulsar. Using the pulsar's motion and
observations from multiple epochs, we have resolved six scattering screens,
five of which are moving with the pulsar and one located in the interstellar
medium. We have determined the scattering properties such as the location,
distance, scattering layer thickness, electron column density, and radius of
curvature for each screen. Among the moving screens, we identified one
colliding cosmic wind shell moving with a speed of $392\pm 26$ km/s and another
possibly related shell-like structure. The remaining three moving screens are
likely to be in the pulsar wind nebulae. The stationary screen is located in
within 1 pc of the solar system.

frequencies and evaluated the refractive index of the medium, which is
approximately unity, indicating that the medium is likely to be plasma. Among
the moving screens, the colliding shell timescale shows evidence of a
dependence on the frequency, indicating that the frequency-averaged line-of-sight
thickness of the shell is less than a radian. The possible shell timescale
indicates that the density of electrons has a cylindrical symmetry about the
pulsar's direction of motion. The scintillation arcs and resolved screens
imply the presence of a pulsar wind nebula (PWN) along this line of sight.

the annotation process of a large number of human annotators over time,
including both human annotators and automated checks on the annotations. We
describe the architecture of MADARi and the experiments conducted to evaluate
its performance. MADARi has successfully supported the annotation of more than

metrics and a user study. MADARi's annotated morphological and spelling

as well as the annotation guidelines, for the benefit of the NLP research
community. The framework itself is not open-sourced due to internal policies.
However, we provide a detailed documentation of it, so that other researchers
can use it as an example when designing their own annotation tools.
  For the analysis, we provide a user study with 12 annotators and a set of
metrics including agreement, f-score, and leakage metrics. The user study
demonstrates that the intuitive interfaces of MADARi make annotating easier and
more enjoyable for human annotators, resulting in higher quality annotations.
The evaluation also shows that MADARi's automated checks further increase the
quality of the annotations.

perform better on Arabic text classification and part-of-speech tagging tasks,
highlighting the importance of high-quality annotated datasets in evaluating
NLP models and achieving better performance.

large number of human annotators over time, along with the high quality of the
annotations and the utility of the annotated dataset, make it a successful

prone to error propagation. End-to-end approaches use only one system to avoid
propagating error, yet are difficult to employ due to data scarcity. We explore
zero-shot translation, which enables translating a pair of languages that is
unseen during training, thus avoid the use of end-to-end ST data. Zero-shot
translation has been shown to work for multilingual machine translation, yet
has not been studied for speech translation. We attempt to build zero-shot ST
models that are trained only on ASR and MT tasks but can do ST task during
inference. The challenge is that the representation of text and audio is
significantly different, thus the models learn ASR and MT tasks in different
ways during training, making it difficult to do zero-shot during inference.
Further, the training data for ASR and MT tasks is in different languages and
domains, thus the models can overfit to the training data rather than
learn general representation. We propose a multi-domain, multi-lingual model
that can do zero-shot ST. The model uses a common representation for text and
audio by using two encoders, one for text and the other for audio, connected to
a shared decoder. The model is trained in a multi-task fashion using only
standard ASR and MT data, but is evaluated on ST task using the Wikipedia
corpus in English and German.

is also able to learn linguistic features, as it learns to translate words

the best suited to describe the scattering of electromagnetic radiation, as
exemplified for an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are then used to
calculate the optical force acting on semiconductor, dielectric or metallic
particles in a wide wavelength range, from the dipolar down to the Mie regimes.
Finally, we calculate the drag force, when a particle is trapped in a laser
beam and move with the laser, and compare it with the calculation of the total
force for an untrapped particle.
  In the dipolar regime (e.g. $r\sim 10 nm$ for a silicon particle) the choice
of the electromagnetic multipoles does not affect the drag force nor the other
components of the force, to a large extent, due to the symmetry of the laser
beam. Moving to the Mie regime (e.g. $r\sim 4 \mu m$ for a silicon particle) the
choice of the multipoles affects the drag force in a significant way, ranging
from 9 to 1 for the Cartesian primitive and spherical multipoles, and from 12 to
3 for the Cartesian irreducible multipoles, depending on the particle
isolation. In between, in the transition regime, the choice of the multipoles
may affect also the other components of the force, as it happens for
asymmetric particles and narrow laser beams.
  Our work stresses the importance of calculating the electromagnetic
multipoles in a Cartesian-spherical combined scheme, not as separate and
independent approaches, and highlights the need for further development of the
theory of irreducible Cartesian multipoles.
  Finally, we remark that the choice of the multipoles may affect also other
physics, e.g. absorption, scattering probability, and radiative cooling.
Therefore, in order to have a complete picture, we report the ratio between the
flux of the incoming laser and the flux of the scattered radiation for the
cartesian primitive, irreducible and spherical multipoles.
  From the above analysis it follows that, in order to have a reliable
prediction of the optical force, also in out of equilibrium conditions, the
spherical multipoles scheme should be used for asymmetric particles only for
wavelength much larger than the particle size.
